The policies do not treat an industry credential as a licensure qualification, do not set a 5000-hour requirement for welding or any CTE area, and do not convert hours into experience credit; experience is counted in full-time calendar months and years, and non-teaching work counts only if it is relevant, paid, documented, at least half-time, and recommended by the employing unit. The specific license level cannot be determined from the policies alone. It depends on whether the person completed an educator preparation program, holds a clear out-of-state license, holds a bachelor's degree, has ever held a North Carolina license, and whether a public school unit requests the license. The CTE-specific provisional path referenced in the policies is defined in LICN-014 and the CTE manual, which are not in the corpus.

key_points.point: Welding is a recognized CTE license area (Trade and Industrial Education - Welding), so the teaching license area itself is available in principle.

Under the CTE exception, an applicant with only a high school diploma or associate's degree may be issued a CTE teaching license, provided all other requirements for the classification sought are met.
The policies do not recognize an industry credential as a licensure qualification. The welding credential does not by itself establish a license level in the corpus.

No hour-based requirement for CTE or welding appears in the policies. Experience credit is counted by full-time calendar months within a fiscal year, or by years, and the policies give no hours-to-years conversion. A 5000-hour figure cannot be converted to experience credit from the corpus.

Any non-teaching work experience counts toward experience credit only if it is at least half-time (20 or more hours per week), completed after age 18, not on-the-job training, paid and documented, directly related to the license area, and recommended by the employing unit. The credit is one year for every two years of relevant work before a bachelor's degree and one year for every year after it. Documentation is needed to determine whether any of the 5000 hours qualify.

Eligibility for each license classification depends on facts the question omits. An initial professional license requires completion of a recognized NC educator preparation program with EPP recommendation, or an out-of-state EPP, or a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of experience. A permit to teach requires a bachelor's degree and no prior NC professional educator license. An emergency license requires a bachelor's degree with at least 18 relevant credit hours, no completed EPP in the area, and no residency eligibility. A residency license requires 24 coursework hours or a passed exam, plus a PSU request.
Exam requirements for welding cannot be confirmed from the corpus. The testing table does not list a welding exam, and the CTE manual it refers to is not in the corpus.

missing_facts_to_ask: Does the applicant hold a bachelor's degree, an associate's degree, or only a high school diploma?
Did the applicant complete a recognized educator preparation program in welding or CTE? If so, in North Carolina or out of state?
Does the applicant hold a clear professional educator license from another jurisdiction, and how many years of licensed teaching experience do they have there?
Has the applicant ever held a North Carolina professional educator license, including a permit or emergency license?
Has the applicant passed any required licensure exam for the welding license area?
Is a public school unit employing the applicant and willing to request a license for them? Which license type is being requested?
How many coursework hours in welding does the applicant have, and at what institution and grade?

Are the 5000 hours full-time or part-time, paid, documented, completed after age 18, free of on-the-job training, directly related to welding, and at least 20 hours per week? Is there documentation of the work and an employer recommendation?
Was any of the 5000 hours spent in military service or in a JROTC role that could trigger a separate credit rule?
What is the specific industry credential, who issued it, and does the employing unit consider it relevant to the welding license area?
false_premises: The draft notes suggest that work hour requirements may differ by CTE area. The policies set no CTE-specific hour requirement. The only hour thresholds are the 15-hour-per-week part-time experience minimum (LICN-006 §I(b)) and the 20-hour-per-week non-teaching minimum (LICN-006 §II(a)).

The question treats an industry credential in welding and 5000 hours of on-the-job experience as qualifying facts. The corpus does not recognize an industry credential or an hour total as a licensure qualification.
out_of_scope_parts: Naming a specific CTE 'license level' such as Class V or a CTE provisional license: LICN-006 mentions Class V CTE licenses and LICN-010 §5(i) lists a Provisional License under LICN-014, but neither is defined in the corpus, and LICN-014 is not included.
The CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual, which LICN-003 §5 refers to for CTE licensure requirements.
Statutory criteria referenced by LICN-019 §1(a), LICN-023 §1(a), and LICN-020, including G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(4a) and (a)(5), which are not in the corpus.
Recognition of industry credentials for licensure, which no policy in the corpus addresses.
Any conversion of the 5000 hours into experience credit beyond the rules quoted in LICN-006.
answer.reviewer_notes: The question is an eligibility-style question, but the facts needed to pick a license level (degree, EPP completion, out-of-state license, NC license history, PSU request) are missing, so the verdict is needs_more_info. Several gaps in the corpus limit the answer: LICN-014 (Provisional License) is cited but not included; 'Class V' CTE licenses appear only in a LICN-006 passage without definition; the CTE manual referenced by LICN-003 is not in the corpus; and the LICN-003 testing table has no welding row, which may reflect a table omission rather than a no-exam rule. The drafter's notes about CTE-specific hour requirements and the industry credential are not supported by the policies. LICN-006 is effective 2025-07-01, earlier than the other policies, but it is the current adopted version. Statutory provisions cited in LICN-019, LICN-020, and LICN-023 were not checked because they are not in the corpus.

question: School social worker with an MSW from NC program, 2 yrs experience, no license yet. Which license and what exam?

answer.reference_answer: A school social worker is a classification of the Student Services Personnel license, a five-year renewable license. An MSW is a master's-level degree and meets the degree requirement, but the applicant must have completed an educator preparation program (EPP) at that level, and the policies do not say whether this North Carolina MSW program is a recognized EPP, so that must be confirmed. The policies do not name a required licensure exam for school social workers; the test table lists none for this classification, so the corpus cannot state which exam applies. The license type depends on exam status: if the applicant has already satisfied any applicable exam requirement before applying, DPI issues a Continuing Professional License; if not, but the applicant otherwise qualifies, DPI issues a three-year nonrenewable Initial Professional License, with the exam attempted in the first year and satisfied by the third year. Two years of experience is not a licensure requirement for this license; it is recorded on the license and governs salary.

key_points.point: A school social worker is one of the classifications of the Student Services Personnel license, which is a five-year renewable license.
A master's degree (M-level) EPP meets the general student services personnel degree level, and the school social worker minimum is a bachelor's degree or higher, so an MSW satisfies both.

Eligibility requires completion of an educator preparation program at the applicable level, and the license is set at the highest degree level at which the EPP was completed. The policies do not say whether a North Carolina MSW program counts as an EPP, so this must be confirmed.

The licensure test table lists no examination for school social workers. It lists school counselor, school psychologist, media coordinator, audiologist, and speech-language pathologist, and the table note says it includes only areas with NCSBE-required exams. The policies therefore do not identify a required exam for this applicant.

Exam timing governs the license type. If the applicant satisfies the applicable exam requirements before initial application, DPI issues a Continuing Professional License. If not, but the applicant otherwise meets the qualifications, DPI issues an Initial Professional License, and the exam must be attempted in the first year and satisfied before or during the third year.
An Initial Professional License is three years and nonrenewable. A Continuing Professional License is five years and renewable.

The student services personnel qualification section sets no years-of-experience requirement. Experience is recorded on the license and is used for salary credit under the experience rules, so the two years do not determine licensure eligibility under these policies.

A complete application requires transcripts and documentation that the applicant completed the EPP, documentation of any applicable exam performance, disclosure of criminal and license history, and the application fee. Applications for state-funded salary must be complete by April 15 of the fiscal year.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the North Carolina MSW program an educator preparation program recognized by the SBE, with EPP completion documentation available as LICN-004 requires?
Has the applicant already satisfied any licensure examination requirement that applies to school social workers, and if so which one? The corpus names none, so confirm with DPI.
Is the applicant employed by a public school unit now, and does the request need to be processed before April 15 to allow state-funded salary?
Does the applicant have any pending or prior criminal charge, conviction, license suspension or revocation, or investigation that must be disclosed?
Does the applicant hold any other professional educator license, in North Carolina or another state, that could affect the application?
false_premises: The draft assumes a specific licensure exam applies to school social workers. The test table in the corpus lists no school social worker exam, so the exam cannot be named from these policies.

The draft note suggests experience requirements may differ. The student services personnel qualification section sets no experience requirement, so the two years of experience do not affect licensure eligibility under these policies.
The draft refers to school services personnel; the policy term is student services personnel.
out_of_scope_parts: Salary placement on the State Salary Schedule and the experience or graduate-degree credit calculation for the MSW and the two years; this would need employment dates and percentage of employment (LICN-006 §I, §V).
The exact application fee for this license. LICN-008 lists general in-state Initial Professional License fees, and the schedule is not specific to student services personnel.
answer.reviewer_notes: Main gap: the test table (LICN-003 §5) has no school social worker row, and its note says it lists only areas with NCSBE-required exams, so no exam is likely required. LICN-012 §9 still refers to applicable exam requirements without defining them for school social workers, so the §9(a) versus §9(b) branch is unclear if no exam applies. Treat the CPL-versus-IPL answer as conditional on exam status. Second gap: the corpus never says whether a North Carolina MSW program is a recognized EPP; if it is not, eligibility under LICN-012 §3 would fail and the answer would change. The draft note said school services personnel; the policy term is student services personnel. Not a conflict: LICN-012 §3 sets an M-level minimum while §5 sets a bachelor's minimum for school social workers, and the MSW meets both. The EPP recommendation requirement in LICN-020 §1(a) and §2 applies to teacher Initial Professional Licenses, not to this student services license, so it was not applied. Teacher CPL requirements in LICN-024 §1(c) (three years of teaching) also do not apply to this classification.

question: school psych candidate, EdS from a non-NASP program, currently working as a psych under a provisional contract. Eligible for NC school psychologist license?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not require a NASP-accredited program, so NASP status does not control eligibility. A school psychologist license requires preparation at the advanced/specialist or doctoral level, and an EdS can meet that level if it was completed through an educator preparation program. That EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent authority where it is based. Whether the candidate can receive an IPL or CPL depends on whether the EPP is NC-recognized or out-of-state and on the school psychologist exam (Praxis 5403, score 155), which must be attempted in the first year and passed before or during the third year. The policies do not recognize a 'provisional contract' as a license, so the analyst should confirm whether the candidate holds any NC professional educator license.

key_points.point: Degree level: a school psychologist license requires preparation at the advanced/specialist or doctoral level, and the EPP must be at the M, S, or D level. An EdS would meet the specialist level if it was completed through an EPP.

NASP accreditation is not a requirement in these policies. The test is whether the EPP is recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business. The license's degree level is set by the highest degree completed at an EPP.

Pathway depends on where the program is based. A North Carolina recognized EPP supports an IPL with EPP recommendation. An EPP based outside North Carolina supports an IPL, and an out-of-state applicant must meet the out-of-state exam or North Carolina exam requirements.

Exam: the school psychologist licensure exam is Praxis 5403 with a required score of 155. Under the school psychologist exam timing rule, the candidate must attempt it during the first year and satisfy it before or during the third year. If the exam is already passed before initial application, the license is a CPL.
A Nationally Certified School Psychologist credential entitles the holder to a CPL. The policies do not say whether the candidate holds it.

The policies do not recognize a 'provisional contract' as a license. Any professional educator employed in a public school must hold or be qualified to hold an NC license, so the candidate's current employment status needs to be checked against the license they actually hold.

missing_facts_to_ask: Was the EdS completed through an educator preparation program, and is that program recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority where it is based?
Is the EPP located in North Carolina or in another jurisdiction?
Does the candidate hold any current NC professional educator license? If so, what type and when does it expire?
What is the 'provisional contract'? Is it a license, or only an employment document?
Has the candidate passed the school psychologist exam (Praxis 5403, score 155) or another required exam? If not, when was it first attempted?
Does the candidate hold a Nationally Certified School Psychologist credential?
Does the candidate hold a clear license from another state, and how many years of licensed experience do they have there?
Is the candidate seeking an IPL or a CPL?
false_premises: The policies do not require NASP program accreditation for a school psychologist license.
'Provisional contract' is not a license type in these policies.
Program accreditation is not the test. The policies use SBE or equivalent-authority recognition of the EPP (LICN-001 §3(d)).
out_of_scope_parts: NASP accreditation standards and whether this specific EdS program is NASP-approved.
Terms of the provisional employment contract.
LICN-014 (Provisional License), cited in LICN-010 and LICN-001 but not in the corpus, so any provisional license basis cannot be confirmed.
Whether the EdS qualifies as a specialist-level degree under the policies, since the policies do not define the EdS.
answer.reviewer_notes: Verdict is needs_more_info because the outcome depends on EPP recognition, program location, and exam status, none of which the question gives. Interpretation: I treated the EdS as a specialist-level (S-level) degree, which the policies do not define. The drafter's accreditation premise is not in the policies. The 'provisional contract' cannot be matched to any license type in the corpus, and LICN-014 is referenced but absent. Note also that LICN-012 §9 timing rules may already be running for a candidate working as a psychologist.

question: media coordinator with an MLS, no teaching experience, wants NC media license. Options?

answer.reference_answer: A media coordinator is a student services personnel classification, so the license is a student services personnel license under LICN-012, not a teacher license, and the policies do not require a teaching license or teaching experience for it. The central requirement is completion of an educator preparation program at the master's level or higher, so the MLS qualifies only if it was completed through a program recognized under the policies; the policies do not say an MLS by itself is enough. The applicant must also satisfy the Media Coordinator licensure exam (Praxis 5312, required score 154). If the exam is passed before application, DPI issues a continuing professional license; if not, the applicant may receive an initial professional license (three years, nonrenewable) and must attempt the exam in the first year and pass it before or during the third year. Teacher-only options such as the permit to teach, emergency license, residency license, and limited license do not apply to this classification. The answer turns on whether the MLS came from a recognized EPP, the exam status, and whether the applicant holds an out-of-state license.

key_points.point: A media coordinator is classified as a student services personnel license area, so the applicable rule is the student services personnel license, not a teacher license.

A student services personnel license requires completion of an educator preparation program at the master's, specialist, or doctoral level. An MLS satisfies the degree level, but the policies require the program to be an EPP, so the MLS must come from a program recognized under the policies.

The applicant's highest degree at an EPP determines the license level, and the license cannot be issued above that level. If the MLS is the highest degree completed through an EPP, the license is at the master's level.
Licensure exam for Media Coordinator (code 076) is Praxis 5312 with a required score of 154.

If the applicant satisfies the exam before applying, DPI issues a continuing professional license. If the applicant has not satisfied it but otherwise qualifies, DPI issues an initial professional license. In either case the exam must be attempted in the first year and satisfied before or during the third year.

The draft's premise that a teaching license is required is not supported. Teaching experience is a condition only for a teacher CPL, and the policies set no teaching-experience requirement for student services personnel.

Teacher-only license types (permit to teach, emergency license, residency license) are issued under the teacher classifications, and the limited license may be issued only for teaching areas and not for student services personnel areas. None of these is a route for a media coordinator.

The application must include official transcripts for the MLS, documentation that the applicant completed an EPP, documentation of exam performance, and the required disclosures. The application fee is $70 for an in-state initial professional license or $100 for an out-of-state one.

missing_facts_to_ask: Was the MLS completed through an educator preparation program recognized by the SBE (or by the equivalent authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP is based), or through a general library-science program that is not an EPP?

Has the applicant passed the Praxis 5312 Media Coordinator exam with a score of at least 154, or does the applicant still need to take it? If the exam is still needed, when does the applicant plan to take it?
Does the applicant hold any current out-of-state or North Carolina professional educator license, and if so, which one and in what status?
Is the position a media coordinator (student services personnel) or a media supervisor (administrative, code 078, Praxis 5412)? Only the coordinator license is covered by the policies cited here.
Is the MLS from a North Carolina institution or from outside North Carolina?
When is the applicant's employing school system planning to hire the applicant, and will a complete application be submitted by April 15 of the fiscal year?
false_premises: A media license may require a teaching license. Media coordinators are student services personnel, and the policy for that license does not require a teaching license.
No teaching experience would matter for this license. Teaching experience is a requirement only for a teacher CPL under LICN-024 §1(c), not for student services personnel.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether a particular MLS program is a recognized EPP. The corpus does not list recognized programs, so the analyst must check the SBE or DPI recognition list.

Mechanics of out-of-state exam recognition for student services personnel. LICN-025 is written around teacher license areas (it cross-references LICN-010), so it is unclear whether it applies to a media coordinator.
State Salary Schedule placement and salary for a media coordinator. The policies address graduate pay only generally (LICN-006 §V) and do not address this classification's pay.
Renewal of the license after it is issued (LICN-032 would apply to a CPL, but the question does not reach that stage).
answer.reviewer_notes: The corpus does not say whether a general MLS is enough or whether the EPP must be specifically a media or library program, so the key question turns on EPP recognition. LICN-012 §9 is the controlling exam rule for student services personnel. LICN-020 §1 (IPL qualifications) is written generally for initial professional educator licenses and was cited for context only; it is not clearly limited to teachers, so the IPL pathway for this classification rests mainly on LICN-012 §9(b). LICN-025 §1 and §2 may or may not extend to student services personnel because it cross-references LICN-010 license areas; treat any out-of-state pathway as uncertain. The draft's 'teaching license' premise is contradicted by LICN-012, and the reviewer should confirm that the analyst means the media coordinator license and not the media supervisor license.

question: Teacher on a Limited License in Latin, 2 years in, teaching at a charter school. Can they get a full RL?

answer.reference_answer: "RL" is not a license type defined in the policies, so the analyst needs to confirm which license is meant. If it is a Residency License, LICN-019 requires a PSU request, G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) (not in the corpus), and either 24 content-area credit hours or a passed licensure exam; the policies give no path from a Limited License to a Residency License. If it is a Continuing Professional License (CPL), the policies require an IPL or residency license first, at least three years of licensed teaching experience (this teacher has two), a passed Latin exam before or during the third year, and Beginning Teacher Support Program completion unless an exception applies. The policies do not expressly provide a direct Limited-to-CPL conversion, and the Limited License has one year left in its three-year term. Whether the charter school counts as a PSU employer also needs confirmation.

key_points.point: "RL" is not a defined license classification in the policies. The closest matches are the Residency License (LICN-019) and the Continuing Professional License (LICN-024), so the question cannot be answered until the intended license is confirmed.
A Limited License is a three-year renewable license for someone who completed an EPP but has not satisfied the licensure exam requirements. At two years in, about one year remains in the term.

A Limited License may only be issued for a teaching license area. Latin is a listed teaching area (special subject, and a secondary area in the test table), so the Latin area itself is not disqualifying.

A Limited License is requested by the governing body of a public school unit under G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(4a), which is not in the corpus. Whether a charter school's governing body qualifies is not stated in the policies; the policies use 'NC LEA or Charter School' in some places and 'PSU governing body' in others.

Under the policies, a CPL requires holding an IPL or a residency license in North Carolina. A Limited License is not listed as a qualifying prior license, so the policies do not provide a direct Limited-to-CPL route. The policies do not expressly prohibit one either.
A CPL also requires at least three years of licensed teaching experience, one year more than this teacher has, and the exam requirement must be met before or during the third year of licensure.
Completion of the Beginning Teacher Support Program is required for a CPL unless an exception applies. The program itself (TCED-016) is not in the corpus.

Latin requires the ACTFL-style Praxis test 5601 with a required score of 146, per the testing table. Whether the teacher has passed it is not stated; passing it is necessary for a CPL and, for a Residency License, is an alternative to the 24-hour coursework path.

To renew a Limited License, the employing PSU must submit an affidavit attesting the teacher is employed, effective, and will be encouraged to pursue a CPL, and the teacher must meet or exceed expected EVAAS growth where data exists. The Limited License is not portable between PSUs.

missing_facts_to_ask: What does 'RL' mean here: a Residency License, a Continuing Professional License, or something else?
Has the teacher passed the Latin licensure exam (Praxis 5601, required score 146), and if so, when?
Is the two years of experience all licensed full-time teaching experience in North Carolina?
When was the Limited License issued, and how much of the three-year term is left?
Did the teacher complete an NC educator preparation program, and was the employer's recommendation made?
Is the charter school governing body treated as a PSU governing body that can request a license for this teacher?
Has the teacher completed or been exempted from the Beginning Teacher Support Program?
Has the teacher completed 24 credit hours of coursework in Latin, if a Residency License is the goal?
false_premises: The question asks about a 'full RL'. No license called RL exists in the policies; the nearest are Residency License and Continuing Professional License.
The draft note says a Limited License may not convert directly. The policies do not contain an express ban; LICN-024 §1(a) simply lists IPL or residency as the prior license for a CPL.
out_of_scope_parts: The statutory criteria in G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(4a) and (a)(5) are not in the corpus.
The Beginning Teacher Support Program requirements in TCED-016 are not in the corpus.
Whether a charter school is a 'public school unit' is not defined in the corpus.
Any policy on converting a Limited License to an IPL is not in the corpus.
answer.computation: Limited License term: 3 years (LICN-001 §2(q)). Elapsed: 2 years. Remaining: 3 - 2 = 1 year. CPL experience requirement: at least 3 years of licensed teaching experience (LICN-024 §1(c)). Shortfall, if the two years are all licensed teaching: 3 - 2 = 1 year.
answer.reviewer_notes: The core ambiguity is the acronym 'RL', which is not defined in the corpus; the answer covers both Residency License and CPL readings. Two gaps exist in the source: the statutory criteria (G.S. 115C-270.20) cited by LICN-019 and LICN-023 are not in the corpus, and the corpus never states whether a Limited License may convert to an IPL or CPL. Whether a charter school counts as a PSU is inferred from usage across LICN-006, LICN-007 and LICN-019, not defined. The answer should not be read as a yes or no on any license.

question: rl holder, 3rd yr, bs in english, never took praxis content test. what happens at end of rl?

answer.reference_answer: A residency license is a one-year license renewable twice, so the third year is its final year. To avoid expiration, the holder must meet the requirements for an initial professional license (IPL) or continuing professional license (CPL), with a recommendation from the educator preparation program (EPP), by June 30 of the third year; a timely conversion takes effect July 1 of the next fiscal year. The IPL requirements in the policy do not include a licensure exam, so an IPL may be possible without the content test if the EPP recommends the holder and the holder otherwise qualifies. A CPL is harder: it requires the exam to be satisfied before or during the third year, a first-year attempt that appears not to have happened, three years of licensed teaching experience, and a Beginning Teacher Support Program, and the policy does not clearly say how the first-year attempt rule applies to residency holders. If no conversion happens by June 30 of the third year, the residency license expires and a later IPL or CPL takes effect only when its requirements are met. The answer turns on the EPP recommendation, which license the holder seeks, teaching experience, and the holder's employment, none of which the question provides.

key_points.point: A residency license is a one-year license renewable twice, so the third year is the last year it can run.
To convert, the holder must meet the IPL or CPL requirements and be recommended by the EPP that prepared them.

If the conversion requirements are met by June 30 of the third year, the IPL or CPL takes effect July 1 of the next fiscal year; if not, the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL takes effect when the requirements are later met.

The IPL requirements (completed recognized NC EPP and EPP recommendation, or out-of-state EPP or license) do not list a licensure exam, so an IPL conversion does not on its face require passing the content test.

The CPL requires the licensure exam to be satisfied before or during the third year and, if not satisfied before the IPL, an attempt at least once during the first year. The holder never tested, so the first-year attempt condition appears unmet; the policy does not expressly address residency holders.
A CPL also requires three years of licensed teaching experience and completion of a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exception applies.
Residency eligibility required either 24 hours of coursework in the content area or passing the exam; since the holder never tested, the policy implies the coursework path was used.
The content test for English (9-12) is listed under LICN-003 as Praxis 5038; the required score cell is malformed in the source.
Reinstatement after a missed renewal is available only if the license has not already been renewed twice, which would likely rule it out for a holder in the third year.

missing_facts_to_ask: Has the holder's EPP completed the program and agreed to recommend conversion (LICN-019 §3(a)(ii))?
Does the holder want an IPL or a CPL, and is a CPL being pursued at all?
How many years of licensed teaching experience does the holder have (LICN-024 §1(c))?
Has the holder completed a Beginning Teacher Support Program, or has out-of-state teaching experience applied (LICN-024 §1(d))?
Did the holder use the 24-hour coursework path for the residency license, and what is the exact license area (for example, English 9-12)?
Is the holder still employed by the PSU, and did the holder renew the residency license twice?
Has the holder attempted any licensure exam at all, including during the first year?
false_premises: The question implies that failing or not taking the content test is what ends the residency license. The policies do not link expiration to the content test; the residency license expires only if the IPL or CPL conversion is not completed by June 30 of the third year (LICN-019 §3(b)), and the test is a CPL requirement, not an IPL requirement.
out_of_scope_parts: How the content test is scored or what the passing score means beyond the table entry
Whether the PSU or the holder can obtain a waiver of the content test outside the stated policies
Salary and experience-credit consequences of the license change
answer.reviewer_notes: The policies do not clearly say whether the LICN-024 first-year attempt requirement applies to residency holders, since that condition is framed around IPL holders; the reference answer treats it as an unresolved ambiguity. The LICN-003 English row's required-score cell reads '5038 - 167' and looks malformed; the score 167 is inferred. LICN-003 §3 refers to 'the end of this section' for current requirements, which is in §5. LICN-019 §1(a)(ii) and §3(a)(i) cross-reference LICN-020 and LICN-024 requirements, so the no-exam IPL answer depends on reading LICN-020 as complete. The question does not state whether the holder completed the EPP, so the answer is conditional.

question: Applicant has a bachelor's in math with a 3.2 GPA, passed Praxis content exam, no ed prep program. Which initial NC license path applies?

answer.reference_answer: A bachelor's in math plus a passed content exam does not by itself establish an initial professional license. The standard initial professional license requires completing an educator preparation program in North Carolina or outside it, or holding an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of experience, and this applicant meets none of those. The GPA is not a licensure criterion in these policies. The likely routes are a residency license, which a public school unit must request for an employee who meets the statutory requirement in G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) (not in this corpus) and who has passed the applicable content exam; a permit to teach, only if the applicant has never held any North Carolina professional educator license and the employing unit requests it; or an emergency license, which is unavailable if the applicant qualifies for a residency license. Which path applies depends on employment by a public school unit, licensure history, and whether the Praxis score meets the required score.

key_points.point: The standard initial professional license (IPL) requires either completion of a North Carolina recognized EPP with EPP recommendation, completion of an out-of-state EPP, or a clear out-of-state license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience. This applicant has no educator preparation program and no stated out-of-state license, so the IPL route does not apply on these facts.
Passing the content exam does not substitute for educator preparation. The add-on route in LICN-013 requires an existing IPL or CPL, so it cannot create a first license.

A residency license may be requested by the governing body of a public school unit that employs the applicant, if the applicant meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and has either 24 hours of content coursework or has passed the applicable licensure examination for that content area. Passing the Praxis content exam satisfies the examination alternative, but the statutory requirement itself is not in the corpus.

A residency license is renewable only if the employing unit documents that the applicant is enrolled in a recognized EPP and is employed as a teacher. The applicant would therefore need to enroll in an EPP to keep the residency license, and the unit must provide the required professional development.

A permit to teach may be requested by the employing unit only if the applicant holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license. It is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be renewed.

An emergency license is available only to an applicant who has not completed a recognized EPP in the area, holds a bachelor's degree with at least 18 relevant credit hours, and does not qualify for a residency license. Because this applicant appears to qualify for a residency license through the passed exam, the emergency license is excluded on these facts, subject to the unknown statutory requirement.

The licensure exam for secondary mathematics is Praxis 5165 with a required score of 159. Whether the applicant passed depends on whether the score met that threshold, which the question does not state.
GPA does not appear as a licensure requirement in the policies in this corpus, so the 3.2 GPA does not change the outcome under these policies.
A limited license is not available on these facts because it requires a prior lateral entry license that the applicant has not been described as holding.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the applicant currently employed by a North Carolina public school unit, and is that unit willing to request a residency license, permit to teach, or emergency license?
Has the applicant ever held any North Carolina professional educator license, including a permit or residency license? A permit to teach requires that they never have.
Did the applicant complete any educator preparation program, in North Carolina or elsewhere? The question says no, but confirm whether any program was partially completed or is in progress.
What Praxis score did the applicant earn on the mathematics content exam, and does it meet the required score for the license area?
Does the applicant hold any out-of-state professional educator license, and if so, is it clear and how many years of licensed teaching experience does the applicant have?

How many relevant credit hours in mathematics does the applicant have, and how many hours of content coursework? These matter if a residency or emergency route depends on coursework rather than the exam.
false_premises: Passing the Praxis content exam with a math degree is enough to qualify for an initial license path on its own. The IPL route requires an educator preparation program or a qualifying out-of-state license, and the exam alone does not create a first license.
The GPA affects licensure eligibility under these policies. No policy in the corpus sets a GPA requirement for any license path.
out_of_scope_parts: The statutory requirement G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which governs residency licenses and is referenced by the limited license rule, is not in the corpus. Whether this applicant meets it cannot be determined from the policies.
The applicant's actual Praxis score is not given, so whether the exam was passed at the required score cannot be confirmed from the question.
answer.reviewer_notes: Read first: the question does not say whether the applicant is employed by a public school unit or has ever held a North Carolina license, and both change which route applies. The answer rests on the policy text, but G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) is cited by LICN-019 and LICN-023 and is not in the corpus, so the residency route is conditional on a requirement this key cannot verify. The drafter's note about GPA is not supported by any policy in the corpus. The question says the exam was passed, but LICN-003 gives a required score of 159 for Praxis 5165, so the score should be checked. The corpus does not cover whether a passed content exam alone supports an add-on or other path beyond what LICN-013 says.

question: Teacher has a CPL in K-6, wants to add a middle grades science area. Has 12 semester hours in science. Enough?

answer.reference_answer: No, 12 semester hours alone do not qualify the teacher to add Middle Grades Science (Grades 6-9) to a CPL. The teacher can add the area either by passing the applicable licensure exam or by completing 24 credit hours of higher-education coursework in science with a grade of C or better in each course. For this area the exam is Praxis 5442 with a required score of 152. If the teacher has already passed that exam with at least 152, the 12 hours do not matter. If not, the teacher needs 12 more qualifying hours to reach 24, provided all 12 existing hours meet the coursework conditions.

key_points.point: A teacher with a CPL may request an add-on to a new teaching license area. Under the policy, the two paths are passing the applicable licensure examination for that area, or completing 24 credit hours of coursework in the area with a grade of C or better in each course.
Twelve semester hours do not satisfy the coursework path, which requires 24 credit hours. The 12 hours alone therefore do not make the teacher eligible.

Middle Grades Science (Grades 6-9) is a recognized teaching license area. The corresponding exam is Praxis 5442 with a required score of 152, so passing that exam is an independent path to the add-on.

The add-on rules do not vary by content area. The only content areas restricted to the exam path are Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, and Middle Grades Science is not one of them, so both paths are open. What varies by area is the exam code and required score.
Because the outcome depends on whether the teacher has already passed Praxis 5442 with at least 152, and on whether the 12 hours are qualifying coursework, the answer is conditional on those facts.

missing_facts_to_ask: Has the teacher already passed Praxis 5442 (Middle Grades Science) with a score of at least 152? If so, the teacher can add the area on that basis.
Are the 12 semester hours from an institution of higher education, all in science, and did the teacher earn a grade of C or better in each course?
Does the teacher have at least 12 additional qualifying hours planned, which would bring the coursework total to 24?
Is the add-on requested to the existing CPL (as the question states), and is the teacher's K-6 license still in good standing?
false_premises: The draft note says add-on credit requirements vary by content area. The general framework in LICN-013 is the same for every area. Only Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum are restricted to the exam path. The content-specific elements are the exam code and score.
The question treats 12 semester hours as a possible threshold. LICN-013 sets 24 credit hours for the coursework path, so 12 is not sufficient on that path.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether a previously taken Praxis 5442 score remains valid or counts toward the add-on. The corpus contains no score-validity or expiration rule.
answer.computation: Coursework path: 24 required minus 12 held = 12 additional qualifying semester hours needed (assuming all 12 existing hours are IHE coursework in science with a grade of C or better). Exam path: 0 additional hours needed if Praxis 5442 is passed with a score of 152 or higher. The CEU conversion in LICN-001 does not apply to add-on credit.
answer.reviewer_notes: The policy says '24 credit hours' while the question says 'semester hours.' This key treats them as the same unit, but the policy does not define credit hours, so confirm if the institution reports quarter hours. The LICN-013 §1 text 'An applicant may only add a license area to an IPL if the applicant has met the licensure examination requirements for the initial license area' applies to IPLs, not CPLs, so it does not bar this CPL holder. Praxis 5442 with score 152 comes from the LICN-003 §5 table under Middle Grades (6-9) Science, code 78300. The corpus does not cover whether the add-on is recorded through a specific application type in LICN-008, so no fee is stated here.

question: Teacher has a Residency License in physical education and wants to switch to elementary ed. Does the RL transfer or start over?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not say that a residency license transfers from physical education to elementary education, and they do not say that changing areas resets the residency timeframe. The only route to a residency license in another area is a new request by the employing PSU under LICN-019 Section 4, which requires the teacher to hold a clear license in another area. A residency license in PE is probably not a clear license under the LICN-001 definition, so that route likely does not apply on these facts, subject to interpretation. Adding elementary education to the existing residency license is barred by LICN-013 Section 3(c). The teacher's eligibility for a new elementary residency license turns on whether the teacher holds a clear license elsewhere and on whether the teacher has 24 credit hours or has passed the elementary examinations.

key_points.point: The policies contain no provision transferring a residency license from one license area to another, and no provision stating that a change of area resets the residency timeframe. The drafter's reset idea is not in the corpus.

A PSU may request a residency license in an additional license area only if the applicant holds a clear license in another area and meets G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) for each requested area. Because the teacher's current license is a residency license, this route likely does not apply unless the teacher holds a separate clear license.
Adding elementary education to the existing PE residency license is not permitted. DPI shall not add teaching license areas under the add-on rule to a residency license.

Initial residency eligibility for a license area requires either 24 hours of coursework in that content area or passing the applicable licensure examination. For elementary, the add-on policy requires examination passage, and the LICN-003 table lists the elementary tests.

The current residency license continues under its own terms. A residency license is a one-year license renewable twice, and to convert it to an IPL or CPL the teacher must satisfy the requirements by June 30 of the third year, or the license expires.
Elementary (K-6) is a valid teacher license area. Physical education is a separate Special Subjects area, so the two are distinct license areas.

missing_facts_to_ask: Does the teacher hold a clear license in any other North Carolina or out-of-state license area? A clear license is needed for the LICN-019 Section 4 route.
Which year of the PE residency license the teacher is in, and when it was first issued, since the three-year conversion window is measured from that point.
Whether the teacher has completed at least 24 credit hours of coursework in elementary education or has passed the required elementary examinations.
Whether the employing PSU is willing to submit a new residency request for elementary education under LICN-019 Section 4.
Whether the teacher is currently employed by the PSU and whether the PSU has requested a residency license in any area before.
false_premises: The draft note says changing area may reset the residency clock. The policies do not address a reset, so the premise is not supported by the corpus.
The question assumes the residency license might transfer. The policies provide no transfer mechanism for residency licenses between license areas.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether a change of area resets the residency timeframe. The policies are silent on this.
The content of G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which LICN-019 Section 4 incorporates. The statute is not in the corpus.
How the residency clock would apply to any new residency license issued in elementary education, since no policy addresses it.
answer.reviewer_notes: Policies are silent on transfer and on any reset of the residency clock, so the draft note is unsupported. Interpretation needed in three places: (1) whether a residency license counts as a clear license under LICN-001 Section 2(f) for purposes of LICN-019 Section 4, which I read as likely not; (2) whether the 24-hour coursework path in LICN-019 Section 1(a)(i) can be used for elementary education, given LICN-013 Section 2(a) requires examinations for elementary add-ons, which may conflict or may apply only to IPL/CPL add-ons; (3) LICN-019 Section 4 cites G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which is not in the corpus. The LICN-019 Section 5(d) text contains a subsection numbering problem (references to 'Subsection (2)(d)'), which does not affect this answer. Reviewer should confirm the clear-license reading before the analyst relies on it.

question: Applicant from Georgia with a Level 5 license, 8 years teaching chemistry, now in NC. Which NC license applies?

answer.reference_answer: The NC policies have no 'Level 5' classification for out-of-state licenses and do not map Georgia's level labels to NC license types, so the Georgia level cannot determine the NC license. Because the applicant has more than three years of licensed teaching experience, the out-of-state initial professional license route (fewer than three years) does not apply. The likely route is a continuing professional license under LICN-025 §2, which requires a clear Georgia license under the LICN-025 definition and either National Board certification or a showing that Georgia's requirements are substantially similar to NC's (an EPP recognized by Georgia and a passing score on a Georgia exam for chemistry). Chemistry is a secondary teaching license area, and NC's own chemistry test requirement is listed in LICN-003. Whether the applicant qualifies cannot be determined from the facts given.

key_points.point: An out-of-state applicant with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience may qualify for a continuing professional license under LICN-025 §2; the IPL route in LICN-025 §1(a) is limited to applicants with fewer than three years, so it does not fit an 8-year teacher. A CPL based on an out-of-state clear license must meet LICN-025.

The Georgia Level 5 label has no mapping in the NC policies. NC teacher license classifications are set by LICN-010 §5, and the degree level for a license is based on the highest degree from an educator preparation program, not on another state's license level.

Criterion one: the Georgia license must be a clear license as defined in LICN-025 §2(a), meaning in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, not revoked or disciplined, no pending unprofessional-conduct investigation in any state, and not surrendered under investigation.

Criterion two: the applicant must either hold National Board for Professional Teaching Standards certification, or Georgia's licensure requirements must be substantially similar to NC's. Substantially similar requires, at minimum, completion of a recognized EPP and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought.

The license area is Secondary Chemistry. For NC licensure, the chemistry test listed in LICN-003 §5 is Praxis 5246 with a required score of 146. The policies do not say how a Georgia exam is matched to that NC score beyond the LICN-025 §2(b)(ii) passing-score requirement.
Exam results for an out-of-state exam must be presented at the time of initial NC licensure, and an out-of-state applicant may not use an out-of-state exam to convert an IPL to a CPL.
The application must include proof of a current valid out-of-state license, documentation of any applicable exam performance, and disclosure of any prior suspension, revocation, or criminal history.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the Georgia license a clear license under LICN-025 §2(a), with no discipline, no pending investigation, no voluntary surrender, and renewable by Georgia?
Does the applicant hold current National Board for Professional Teaching Standards certification?

Does Georgia require an educator preparation program recognized by Georgia and a passing score on a Georgia exam for chemistry (the substantially similar test)? If so, did the applicant pass it, and what was the score?
Was the 8 years of teaching chemistry done under a Georgia professional educator license (licensed experience), or was any of it unlicensed?
What is the applicant's highest degree and which EPP completed it, and is that EPP recognized?
Has the applicant ever held an NC professional educator license?
Is the applicant employed by an NC public school unit now, and is the applicant an active-duty servicemember or spouse (which would trigger LICN-028)?
false_premises: The Georgia 'Level 5' label maps to an NC license level. The NC policies contain no Level 5 classification and no out-of-state level mapping, so the NC license cannot be derived from the Georgia label.
The question assumes one NC license applies. The policies do not give a single answer until the clear-license, NBPTS or substantially-similar, and exam facts are known.
out_of_scope_parts: Georgia's own licensing rules, including what a Level 5 license means and whether it is clear under Georgia law.
Whether the BTSP requirement in LICN-024 §1(d) applies to a CPL granted through LICN-025; the policies do not say.
CPL application fee: LICN-008 lists an out-of-state initial professional license fee of $100 but no CPL fee for out-of-state applicants.
Alternative NC licenses (permit to teach, emergency, residency, limited) are not evaluated here because they depend on whether the applicant has ever held an NC license and on PSU requests.
answer.reviewer_notes: The question is not answerable as posed: the answer turns on facts the question omits (clear license status, NBPTS, Georgia's requirements, exam score, degree and EPP). Interpretive points: (1) LICN-025 §2 says the applicant 'must meet both' criteria, and §2(b) joins NBPTS and substantially similar with 'or'; I read criterion two as satisfied by either route. (2) The 'clear license' definition in LICN-025 §2(a) differs from LICN-001 §2(f); LICN-025 adds a renewability requirement and LICN-001 adds a no-additional-exams requirement, so reviewers should not treat them as identical. (3) LICN-025 §2(b)(ii) says passing score 'for each license area which licensure is sought under LICN-010'; the wording looks garbled ('which' for 'for which'), but the meaning is clear enough. (4) The LICN-003 §5 table has chemistry only as Secondary Chemistry (code 330, test 5246, score 146). (5) 'Licensed teaching experience' in LICN-025 §2 is not defined; I have assumed it means experience under a license. (6) LICN-024 §3 routes clear-license-in-other-jurisdiction CPLs to LICN-025, but LICN-024 §1(d) BTSP language is not addressed in LICN-025, so this is flagged as out of scope.

question: Teacher from Texas with a standard certificate in theatre arts, 2 years experience, wants NC license in theatre. Route?

answer.reference_answer: With only two years of licensed experience, the teacher falls under the out-of-state initial professional license (IPL) route, not the continuing professional license (CPL) route, which requires more than three years. The IPL is available if the teacher holds a license in the corresponding area (theatre arts) from Texas or completed an educator preparation program recognized in Texas. Theatre arts is a North Carolina license area, and the LICN-003 testing table lists it among areas with no required NC licensure exam, so the draft premise about a specific NC content test appears incorrect. The policies do not say how the out-of-state exam rule applies when no NC exam is required, so the analyst should confirm that point. The policies do not use the term standard certificate, so whether the Texas credential is a clear license should be verified. Out-of-state exam results must be presented at initial licensure, cannot be used to convert the IPL to a CPL later, and a Texas-based teacher must still meet North Carolina conversion requirements such as the Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exemption applies.

key_points.point: With fewer than three years of licensed experience, an out-of-state applicant qualifies for an IPL, not a CPL; the CPL route requires more than three years.

To qualify for the IPL, the teacher must either hold a license in the corresponding license area (theatre arts) in Texas or have completed an educator preparation program recognized by Texas where the EPP is located.
Theatre Arts is a recognized North Carolina teacher license area under the Special Subjects classification.

The LICN-003 testing table footnote states that Theatre Arts (108) is among the content areas without required NC licensure examinations, so the premise that NC requires a specific theatre content test is not supported by the policies.

For an IPL in an area other than Elementary or Special Education General Curriculum, the teacher must either pass an out-of-state exam for that area in the examining jurisdiction or satisfy the applicable NC exam requirements before or during the third year, having attempted them in the first year. Because no NC exam is listed for theatre arts, how this prong applies is unclear from the text.
If the teacher relies on an out-of-state exam result, the evidence must be presented at the time of initial NC licensure.

The policies do not define standard certificate. The CPL route requires a clear license as defined in the policies (good standing, renewable, no revocation, discipline, or pending investigation, and no surrender under investigation), so the Texas credential's status should be confirmed.

The IPL is a three-year nonrenewable license. Converting it to a CPL later requires a NC IPL, three years of licensed teaching experience, exams satisfied as required, and a Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exemption applies. An out-of-state applicant cannot use out-of-state exam results to make that conversion.

The application must include the required documentation, including out-of-state license proof and exam performance documentation, and the fee for an out-of-state initial professional license is listed as $100.
The degree level on the license is set by the highest EPP degree completed, so the teacher's degree level must be confirmed.

missing_facts_to_ask: Does the Texas credential cover theatre arts as the corresponding license area, and is it a clear license under the policy definition (good standing, renewable, no discipline or pending investigation)?
Did the teacher complete an educator preparation program recognized by Texas, and at what degree level?
Did the teacher pass a Texas exam in theatre arts, and what score?
Are the two years licensed teaching experience in Texas, and has the teacher completed a Beginning Teacher Support Program or does an exemption apply?
Does the teacher plan to seek the IPL now and convert to a CPL later, and is the teacher employed by a North Carolina PSU?
false_premises: The draft note says theatre may need a specific content test in NC. LICN-003 lists Theatre Arts (108) among content areas without required NC licensure examinations, so the policies do not show a specific NC theatre test requirement.
out_of_scope_parts: Texas certification requirements and whether a Texas standard certificate is equivalent to a clear license under Texas law.
Content of any Texas exam and whether it corresponds to the NC theatre arts area.
Requirements of the Beginning Teacher Support Program under TCED-016, which is not in the corpus.
answer.reviewer_notes: The main premise is the NC exam requirement for theatre arts. LICN-003's footnote says Theatre Arts (108) has no required licensure exam, which conflicts with the drafter's note. The text of LICN-025 §1(b) assumes an applicable NC exam, so the second prong may be empty for this area. The answer treats that as an ambiguity rather than a clear rule. The term standard certificate does not appear in the policies, so clear-license status is unverified. LICN-025 covers out-of-state applicants, but LICN-020 §1(c) and LICN-010 §2 may also bear on degree-level and EPP questions, and were not fully worked through. TCED-016 is referenced but not in the corpus.

question: candidate w/ 15 yrs exp in florida, cert in ESOL, wants nc license. which one?

answer.reference_answer: Fifteen years of experience rules out the out-of-state initial professional license, which is limited to applicants with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience. The applicable path is a continuing professional license (CPL) in the ESOL teacher license area, if the candidate holds a clear license from Florida and either holds National Board certification or Florida's requirements are substantially similar to North Carolina's (a recognized educator preparation program plus a passing out-of-state exam for ESOL). In North Carolina, ESOL is a K-12 special subject teacher license area, not a separate license type. The policies do not confirm whether this candidate qualifies, so the analyst needs to confirm the facts listed in missing_facts_to_ask.

key_points.point: Fifteen years of experience places the candidate outside the out-of-state initial professional license, which applies only to applicants with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience.

The out-of-state CPL route applies to applicants with more than three years of licensed professional educator experience who hold a clear license from another jurisdiction and meet either the National Board certification option or the substantially similar requirements option.

Clear license under the out-of-state rule requires good standing, renewability by the issuing authority, no revocation or discipline, no pending unprofessional-conduct investigation, and no surrender under investigation. The candidate's Florida credential must be checked against each element.

Under the substantially similar option, the candidate must have completed an educator preparation program recognized by the state where it is located and passed an out-of-state exam for each license area sought. The policies do not name the Florida ESOL exam, so the analyst must confirm which exam was passed and its score.

ESOL is a K-12 special subject teacher license area in North Carolina. The NC required test is Praxis 5362 with a required score of 155, which is relevant if the candidate must satisfy NC examination requirements rather than rely on the out-of-state option.

Teacher licenses require completion of an educator preparation program at a stated degree level, and the license is issued only at the highest degree level completed, so the candidate's degree level and EPP must be confirmed.

A CPL from the out-of-state route must be issued under the teacher CPL rules, and the Beginning Teacher Support Program requirement in the general CPL rule is not the path for out-of-state clear-license applicants.

missing_facts_to_ask: Were all 15 years of experience served as a licensed professional educator, as opposed to unlicensed or non-teaching work?

Does the candidate hold a current clear Florida license, or only an ESOL certification or endorsement on a license? Is it in good standing, renewable by Florida, and free of discipline or pending investigations?
Does the candidate hold National Board for Professional Teaching Standards certification?
Which educator preparation program prepared the candidate, at what degree level (bachelor's, master's, specialist, or doctoral), and is that program recognized by Florida?
Did the candidate pass a Florida ESOL exam or other out-of-state exam for ESOL, and what score was earned?
Is the candidate seeking only ESOL, or other teaching license areas as well?
Is the candidate a servicemember or spouse of a servicemember with military orders to North Carolina? If so, LICN-028 may apply.
false_premises: The draft notes suggest ESOL may fall under a specific North Carolina license or endorsement. The policies treat ESOL as a K-12 special subject license area on a teacher license (LICN-010 §6(d)(xii)), and the term endorsement does not appear in the corpus.
out_of_scope_parts: Florida's own licensing requirements and whether its ESOL credential meets NC clear-license standards in substance; the corpus does not describe Florida's rules.
Whether the candidate's EPP is recognized by Florida; the corpus does not list recognized programs.
Salary placement for the 15 years of Florida experience; LICN-006 addresses experience credit for North Carolina service and does not address out-of-state years.
Application fee for an out-of-state CPL; the fee table in LICN-008 lists an out-of-state IPL fee and other items but no separate out-of-state CPL line.
answer.reviewer_notes: The question is terse and ambiguous: 'which one' may mean license type, but the policies answer it as a route (CPL under LICN-025 §2) rather than a license name. The draft's 'endorsement' is not a corpus term; ESOL is treated as a license area. LICN-025 §2(b)(ii) says passing an 'applicable exam' for each license area but does not name the exam for ESOL; this reads as requiring a passing score on an out-of-state exam in that area, which we interpret as a Florida ESOL exam, but the corpus does not state this explicitly. LICN-001 §2(f) defines clear license without a renewability element, while LICN-025 §2(a) adds renewability and says it applies 'for purposes of this Rule'; we applied the LICN-025 definition. The LICN-003 ESOL test (Praxis 5362, score 155) is an NC requirement that may not apply to an out-of-state applicant who uses the out-of-state option. No definition of endorsement appears in the corpus. The answer is conditional on facts the analyst has not supplied.

question: Teacher holds a Permit to Teach in computer science, teaching under it for 3 years. Can it be renewed?

answer.reference_answer: No. A Permit to Teach cannot be renewed or extended. It is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested, and the length of time the educator has taught under it does not change that. The policies do not say whether a new permit may be requested for a later fiscal year. Any new request would have to meet the permit eligibility conditions again, including that the applicant has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license. The policies also do not address how the educator could move to a different license type.

key_points.point: A Permit to Teach cannot be renewed or extended.
The permit is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested (fiscal year runs July 1 through June 30), so the three years of teaching under it do not extend its validity.

A permit may only be requested by the employing PSU's governing body for an applicant who holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license. Any new permit request would need to meet these conditions again.

For State Salary Schedule purposes, a permit is certified at the A-level with zero years of experience regardless of education or prior work experience. The policies do not state whether years taught under a permit count toward experience credit for a later license.
The policies do not address a conversion path from a permit to a different license type, or whether a permit may be reissued for later fiscal years.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the analyst asking about the permit's renewal only, or is the educator seeking a different license type now (for example, an initial professional license)?
Has the educator ever held any North Carolina professional educator license, including a previous permit or license in another area?
Was a new permit requested for each fiscal year, or was the permit issued once for one fiscal year?
out_of_scope_parts: Whether the educator may obtain a new permit for a later fiscal year. The policies do not say whether reissuance is allowed, and the answer turns on the LICN-017 §1 conditions.
Whether an IPL, CPL, or other license in computer science can be obtained from the permit, or what requirements would apply. LICN-017 does not state a conversion path.
Whether the 3 years of teaching count toward experience credit for salary on a later license. LICN-006 governs experience credit, but the policies do not directly link permit service to it.
answer.reviewer_notes: The core answer is clear: LICN-017 §2 bars renewal or extension, and the 3-year teaching period is irrelevant to that. The drafter's note that permits have time limits is correct. Note that the policies do not say whether a fresh permit could be requested each fiscal year. Also, computer science is not listed as a separate secondary area in LICN-010 (only Career and Technical Education 'Computer Science and Information Technology Education'), but that does not affect the renewal answer.

question: Applicant has an NC Initial Professional License in music, wants to add an EC area. Has 9 semester hours in EC. Eligible?

answer.reference_answer: Nine semester hours of EC coursework do not qualify the applicant by themselves. An NC IPL holder may add a teaching area only if the applicant has already met the licensure exam requirements for the initial area (music), and then either passes the licensure exam for the EC area or completes 24 credit hours in that area with a grade of C or better in each course. Nine hours is 15 short of the 24-hour route. If the EC area is Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, coursework cannot be used at all and only the exam route applies. Eligibility therefore depends on whether the applicant has passed the music exam and the EC exam, which the question does not state.

key_points.point: An IPL can be added to only if the applicant has already met the licensure exam requirements for the initial license area. Here that is music, so whether the applicant passed the music exam is a threshold condition.

A teaching area can be added in one of two ways: (a) satisfy the applicable licensure exam requirements for that area, or (b) complete 24 credit hours of coursework in the area from an institution of higher education with a grade of C or better in each course.
Nine semester hours does not satisfy the coursework route, which requires 24 credit hours. The applicant would be 15 hours short, so the 9 hours alone do not make the applicant eligible.

If the EC area is Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, it is one of the two areas that can be added only by satisfying the licensure exam requirements, not by coursework. The applicant's 9 hours would not count toward adding it.

If the EC area is a different EC license area (for example Adapted Curriculum or Learning Disabled), the policy text does not bar the coursework route, but the 24-credit-hour threshold still applies, so 9 hours is insufficient.

The exam requirements for the EC area are listed in the LICN-003 §5 table. The EC General Curriculum rows in that table are duplicated and partly garbled, so the exact exam set should be verified before a final determination.

missing_facts_to_ask: Has the applicant satisfied the licensure exam requirements for the music area (LICN-003 §5 lists Music, test 5114, required score 162)?
Which EC license area is sought: Exceptional Children: General Curriculum, or another EC area such as Adapted Curriculum or Learning Disabled?
Has the applicant passed the required licensure exam(s) for the EC area, and with what scores?

If the coursework route is intended: are the 9 hours from an institution of higher education, each course graded C or better, and all in the EC license area? Does the applicant plan to complete 24 credit hours total?
Confirm the NC IPL is an in-state license and is still valid.
answer.computation: Coursework route under LICN-013 §1(b) requires 24 credit hours. Applicant has 9 semester hours. 24 minus 9 equals 15 additional credit hours still needed. This assumes one semester hour counts as one credit hour; the policy does not state a conversion, and no source addresses it.
answer.reviewer_notes: The draft note that the IPL may restrict adding areas is directionally right, but the restriction is in LICN-013 (add-on areas for IPL or CPL holders), not in the IPL policy LICN-020. Read first: the answer turns on which EC area is meant and whether exams were passed, which the question does not state. LICN-013 §2(b) names only Exceptional Children: General Curriculum as exam-only; other EC areas are not in §2, so the coursework route is technically open to them. LICN-013 uses 'credit hours' while the question says 'semester hours'; the policy does not define a conversion, so this was assumed to be equivalent. The LICN-003 §5 table has duplicated and garbled rows for Special Education: General Curriculum (including the math entry '227 150'), so the exact exam set for EC General Curriculum is unclear from the corpus and should be checked against the source. The corpus does not address the music IPL's expiration timing, which is outside this question.

question: Teacher is a former military educator with 8 years experience teaching in DoD schools, no NC license. Which NC license applies?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not say that DoD school teaching counts as licensed experience or as a state license, so the answer depends on facts the analyst has not given. The key split is three years of licensed teaching experience in a jurisdiction. With fewer than three years and a clear out-of-state license, or a qualifying EPP, the teacher would qualify for an Initial Professional License. With more than three years, a clear out-of-state license, and either National Board certification or substantially similar licensing requirements (a recognized EPP and a passing out-of-state exam for the area), the teacher would qualify for a Continuing Professional License. If the teacher has no clear license and no qualifying EPP, only the Permit to Teach, Emergency License, or Residency License routes remain, and each requires a request from a North Carolina public school unit employer and has its own conditions. Military service matters only for salary credit under LICN-006 (if it was active-duty instructional service) or for LICN-028 (if the teacher is still active duty or a spouse with North Carolina orders).

key_points.point: The policies do not address DoD schools. They do not say whether DoD teaching counts as licensed teaching experience or as a licensing jurisdiction, so the 8 years cannot be treated as qualifying experience on the policy text alone.

The 8 years matters only through the three-year thresholds. An IPL route applies with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in the other jurisdiction, and a CPL route requires more than three years of licensed professional educator experience. If the 8 years were licensed teaching in one jurisdiction, the CPL years test would be met.

Out-of-state IPL: the teacher may qualify with a clear license in another jurisdiction and fewer than three years of licensed experience there, or with an EPP recognized by the jurisdiction where it is located. Elementary and Special Education: General Curriculum require a North Carolina exam by the end of year three regardless of out-of-state exam results.

Out-of-state CPL: the teacher needs a clear license (in good standing, renewable, with no discipline or pending investigation), and either a National Board certification or licensure requirements substantially similar to North Carolina's (a recognized EPP and a passing out-of-state exam for each license area sought).
Exam evidence must be presented at initial licensure, and an out-of-state exam result cannot be used to convert an IPL to a CPL.

Routes without a clear out-of-state license: an IPL can be issued on completion of a North Carolina recognized EPP (with the EPP recommendation), and a teacher license generally requires EPP completion at a degree level. The Permit to Teach requires a bachelor's degree, never having held any North Carolina professional educator license, and a request from the employing public school unit; it is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year and cannot be renewed. The Emergency License requires a bachelor's with at least 18 relevant credit hours, no completed recognized EPP in the area, and not qualifying for a Residency License. The Residency License requires meeting G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which is not reproduced in the corpus, plus 24 coursework hours or a passed exam.

Military service: LICN-028 special provisions apply to an active-duty servicemember or spouse with a North Carolina duty station, and to a covered license from another state held by someone relocating under military orders. The word 'former' suggests this may not apply, so the analyst should confirm current status.

Salary credit only: military instructional service earns one year of experience credit for every two years of full-time instructional duty only while on active military duty, and only for veterans first employed by a North Carolina LEA on or after July 1, 2014. This affects salary, not license type.

missing_facts_to_ask: Does the teacher hold a current clear license from any other state or jurisdiction? Is it in good standing, renewable, with no discipline or pending investigation?
How many years of licensed teaching experience (licensed in a jurisdiction, not just employed) does the teacher have, and in which jurisdiction? Did the DoD years count as licensed teaching?
Is the teacher's 8 years more or less than three licensed years, and is exactly three years possible?
Did the teacher complete an educator preparation program? Where, at what degree level, and is it recognized by the jurisdiction where it is located?
Does the teacher hold National Board certification?
Has the teacher passed an out-of-state exam for the license area sought? Which area(s) and grade level(s)?
Which North Carolina license area is sought (e.g., teaching area, grade band)?
Is the teacher currently employed by a North Carolina public school unit, and will the employer request a license?
Does the teacher hold a bachelor's degree? Does it include at least 18 relevant credit hours?
Has the teacher ever held any North Carolina professional educator license?
Is the teacher currently on active military duty, or is the teacher a spouse of an active-duty servicemember with North Carolina orders? Does the teacher hold a covered license from another state?
Were the DoD teaching duties performed on active military duty as instructional service, and when was the teacher first employed by a North Carolina LEA?
false_premises: The question presumes that 8 years of DoD teaching experience alone determines which North Carolina license applies. Under the policies, eligibility turns on out-of-state clear-license status, licensed teaching years in a jurisdiction, EPP completion, and exam or National Board status, none of which DoD service alone establishes.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether DoD schools are a recognized licensing jurisdiction, or whether DoD service counts as licensed teaching experience. The policies do not address DoD schools.
Statutory qualifications in G.S. 115C-270.20, which LICN-019, LICN-023, and LICN-028 cite. The text is not in the corpus.
Beginning Teacher Support Program requirements under TCED-016, which LICN-024 cites. The text is not in the corpus.
Federal servicemember law beyond what LICN-028 incorporates by reference.
Recognition of a foreign or other-state EPP beyond the rule in LICN-025 §1(a)(ii).
Salary placement details beyond the experience credit rules in LICN-006.
