(5) The residency-to-IPL/CPL timing rules come from LICN-019 §3 and LICN-024 §1(b) rather than a residency-specific test rule, so I flagged the interpretation.

question: Are there any exemptions from the Praxis content test for teachers with certain degrees?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not provide a general exemption from the licensure content test based on degree level. Degree level determines which license level an applicant can receive, not whether the content test is required. There is one narrow waiver: no test is required for the Academically or Intellectually Gifted license if it is earned through a recognized Educator Preparation Program, though an applicant may add the area by passing the Praxis Gifted Education test 5358 with a minimum score of 157. Separately, a teacher can add a teaching area to an existing IPL or CPL by completing 24 credit hours of coursework with grades of C or better instead of passing the test, but this does not apply to Elementary Education or Exceptional Children: General Curriculum. The analyst should confirm the specific license area and the applicant's license status before applying any of these rules.

key_points.point: No degree-based exemption from the licensure content test appears in the policies. Degree level sets the license level an applicant can hold, and the testing requirements are set by license area.

The only test waiver in the policy tables is for Academically or Intellectually Gifted (code 88087), which requires no test if the license is earned through a recognized Educator Preparation Program. This is tied to program completion in the area, not to degree level.
Teachers who want to add an AIG area without program completion may pass Praxis Gifted Education test 5358 with a minimum score of 157.

Applicants with only a high school diploma or associate's degree may receive a teaching license in CTE, JROTC, or Safety and Driver Education, but only if they meet all other requirements for the license classification. The policy does not state that this waives testing.

To add a new teaching area to an existing IPL or CPL, an applicant may complete 24 credit hours of coursework in the area with a grade of C or better in each course, as an alternative to the exam. Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum must be added by exam only.

An out-of-state applicant may use an out-of-state exam pass, and for certain areas must still satisfy North Carolina examination requirements. This is a jurisdiction-based route, not a degree-based exemption.

missing_facts_to_ask: Which license area or areas is the teacher seeking, or already holds?
Is the teacher applying for an initial license or adding an area to an existing IPL or CPL?
Did the teacher complete a recognized North Carolina Educator Preparation Program in the area, and at what degree level?
If the question is about an out-of-state teacher, what jurisdiction issued their license and did they pass an out-of-state exam?
Does the teacher's current license status (IPL, CPL, residency, limited) affect whether an add-on is possible?
false_premises: The question assumes exemptions from the Praxis content test depend on degree. The policies do not tie test requirements to degree level; they tie them to license area and, for the AIG area, to completing a recognized program.
answer.reviewer_notes: The only exemption-like text is a footnote (**) to the AIG row in the LICN-003 §5 table, marked as 'none**'. The table formatting is garbled, so the reviewer should check the source for exact wording. The answer treats 'recognized EPP completion' as a program-based waiver, not a degree-based one, and the policies do not define 'recognized' beyond LICN-001 §3(d). The LICN-013 coursework route is an add-on alternative, not an initial-license exemption, and the answer flags that difference. LICN-003 §4 has truncated text in the PLT sentence, but it is not relevant to this question.

question: How much teaching experience counts toward moving up a license level?

answer.reference_answer: The policies define experience credit for salary purposes in LICN-006. Full-time work in a school unit for at least six calendar months within one fiscal year earns one year of credit. Part-time work counts only at a minimum of 15 hours per week, and partial full-time and part-time periods can be combined into one year when they total six full-time calendar months. Tutoring, clerical work, substitute teaching, leaves of absence, and service in a one-teacher private school do not count. The policies do not say that experience moves a license up a level. License level follows the degree level completed (LICN-010 and LICN-011), and converting an IPL to a CPL requires at least three years of licensed teaching experience along with the exam and induction requirements in LICN-024. Before giving a specific figure, confirm which level change is meant (salary placement or IPL-to-CPL conversion) and the details of the service.

key_points.point: For salary purposes, full-time work in a school unit of at least six calendar months within one fiscal year (July 1 through June 30) earns one year of experience credit.
Part-time work counts only at a minimum of 15 hours per week; one year is earned when part-time experience totals six calendar months of full-time experience in a single fiscal year.
Partial years of full-time or part-time experience can be combined for experience credit.

Tutoring, clerical paraprofessional, and substitute teaching are not recognized as professional educator experience credit; leave-of-absence periods are not credited; service in a one-teacher private school is excluded.
Experience credit for a single year served in two or more school administrative units is allowed unless the SBE has been advised the contract was willfully breached during that school year.
License level is tied to the degree level at which the applicant completed an educator preparation program, not to years of experience.

To convert an IPL to a CPL, a teacher must have at least three years of licensed teaching experience, along with the exam requirement and Beginning Teacher Support Program unless an exemption applies.
For out-of-state applicants, fewer than three years of licensed experience qualifies for an IPL and more than three years may qualify for a CPL.
The policies do not define 'licensed teaching experience' for the three-year CPL threshold or state whether LICN-006 salary credit controls that count.

missing_facts_to_ask: Which move is meant: salary placement on the State Salary Schedule, conversion from IPL to CPL, or another license level change?
Position type: teacher, administrator, or student services personnel?
Dates of service by fiscal year (July 1 to June 30), and for each period whether it was full-time or part-time (percentage of employment and hours per week).
Whether the service was in a North Carolina public school unit, a one-teacher private school, college teaching, out of state, or as a substitute, tutor, or clerical worker.
Whether any period was a leave of absence.
Whether the educator served in two or more school administrative units in the same school year, and if so whether the contract was willfully breached.
Current license type (IPL, CPL, residency, limited, or other) and whether the educator holds a clear out-of-state license.
false_premises: The question assumes experience counts toward moving up a license level. The policies tie license level to degree level (LICN-010, LICN-011, LICN-012). The LICN-006 experience credit governs salary placement. For IPL-to-CPL conversion, the policies require three years of licensed teaching experience plus exam and induction requirements (LICN-024).
The term 'license level' is not defined in the corpus.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether out-of-state teaching experience counts for salary experience credit: LICN-006 is written for service in school units and does not address out-of-state service.
Whether the three-year CPL threshold in LICN-024 counts out-of-state experience, beyond the BTSP exemption in LICN-024 §1(d)(i) and the out-of-state rules in LICN-025.
Exact salary schedule placement amounts or pay levels; the policies do not provide salary amounts.
answer.computation: Policy definition (LICN-006 §I(a)): a calendar month equals (days employed divided by days in the pay period) multiplied by the employee's percentage of employment. Illustration, assuming partial periods combine under LICN-006 §I(c): 4 full-time calendar months plus 4 calendar months at 50 percent employment equals 4 + (4 x 0.5) = 6 full-time-equivalent months, which is one year of experience credit within one fiscal year. This is my interpretation. The policy does not state whether a 50 percent appointment meets the 15-hour-per-week minimum for part-time work, so that must be verified.
answer.reviewer_notes: The question is ambiguous. 'License level' is not a defined term, and the answer depends on whether the analyst means salary placement (LICN-006) or IPL-to-CPL conversion (LICN-024). The assistant should ask rather than invent a threshold for advancing license levels. LICN-006 is effective 2025-07-01, older than most of the series (2026-07-01), but it is the current adopted version in the corpus. LICN-024 §1(c) requires 'three years of licensed teaching experience' without defining it or saying whether LICN-006 credit counts. LICN-020 §1(c) uses 'fewer than three years' and LICN-025 §2 uses 'more than three years', so exactly three years is not addressed. The computation example is my interpretation of combining partial years and is not stated in the policy.

question: Does a license expire on a fixed date or on a cycle tied to the holder's birthday?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not tie license expiration to the holder's birthday. Under LICN-001, every license expires on June 30 of the calendar year in which it is set to expire, unless it is renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy. Continuing professional licenses for teachers, administrators, and student services personnel are renewed on a five-year renewal cycle. Some license types have fixed terms instead: an initial professional license is three years and nonrenewable, and permits to teach and emergency licenses are valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which they were requested. The policies do not say how the start of an individual's five-year cycle is set, so the exact expiration year for a given holder has to come from that holder's license record.

key_points.point: Licenses expire on a fixed date: June 30 of the calendar year in which the license is set to expire, unless it is renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy.

Renewal is on a five-year renewal cycle for continuing professional licenses held by teachers, administrators, and student services personnel. A renewal cycle is the five-year period between renewals of a CPL.

Some license types have fixed terms rather than renewal cycles: an initial professional license is three years and nonrenewable; permits to teach and emergency licenses are valid until June 30 of the fiscal year requested and cannot be extended or renewed; a lifetime license requires no renewal.
The policies contain no provision that ties expiration or renewal timing to the holder's birthday.

missing_facts_to_ask: Which license type the holder has (for example CPL, IPL, permit to teach, or emergency license), since the expiration rule differs by type.
The expiration year shown on the holder's current license, to determine when the June 30 expiration or five-year renewal cycle falls.
false_premises: The draft implies a license may expire on a cycle tied to the holder's birthday. The policies do not say this; expiration is set to June 30 (LICN-001 §3(g)).
answer.reviewer_notes: LICN-001 §3(g) says June 30 of the calendar year, while LICN-017 and LICN-018 use June 30 of the fiscal year. Both end on June 30, so the date does not conflict, but the policies use two different year labels. The corpus does not explain how the start of a five-year renewal cycle is set, so the exact expiration year for a given holder cannot be derived from policy text alone.

question: What's the minimum GPA required for an NC teaching license?

answer.reference_answer: The LICN policies in the corpus do not set a minimum GPA for any North Carolina teaching license, so no number can be given from them. The policies do require completion of a recognized educator preparation program at a specified degree level, plus passing the applicable licensure examinations with the score thresholds in LICN-003 for most initial and continuing licenses. Official transcripts are required for degrees, but no GPA figure is specified. Any GPA threshold would have to come from a source outside this corpus, which should be checked before the analyst relies on one.

key_points.point: The LICN policies in the corpus contain no minimum GPA requirement for a teaching license, so they cannot answer the question with a number.

A teacher license generally requires completion of an educator preparation program at a specified degree level (bachelor's, master's, specialist, or doctoral), and an applicant is only eligible at the highest degree level completed.

An initial professional license requires either completion of a recognized North Carolina EPP with EPP recommendation, completion of an EPP based outside North Carolina, or an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of licensed teaching experience in that jurisdiction.

The numeric thresholds in the policies are licensure exam scores, not grade-point averages. Continuing licensure generally requires passing the applicable exams before or during the third year of licensure.
Degree verification uses official transcripts with an EPP completion documentation. The policies require the transcripts but do not specify a GPA that must appear on them.

missing_facts_to_ask: Which license classification the analyst means (for example initial professional, continuing professional, residency, or another type), since the policies set different qualifications for each.
Whether the applicant completed a North Carolina EPP, an out-of-state EPP, or holds an out-of-state clear license.
Where the analyst encountered the GPA figure (for example an EPP admission or completion standard, a district rule, or a non-LICN source), since that source is outside this corpus.
false_premises: The question presumes a minimum GPA exists for an NC teaching license. The LICN policies in the corpus set no GPA requirement, so this premise cannot be confirmed from them.
out_of_scope_parts: Any minimum GPA for a teaching license or for admission to or completion of an educator preparation program. The corpus does not address GPA, and policies referenced in it (such as TCED-015 and TCED-016) are not included in the corpus.
answer.reviewer_notes: Searched all LICN policies in the corpus for GPA, grade point, and quality-point terms; none appear. The silence is therefore a substantive finding, not a gap in the snapshot. Answer is confined to the corpus; no outside knowledge was used. The question is a lookup in form but unanswerable in substance, so it was re-labeled as unanswerable. The drafter's note about possible pathway-specific GPA rules is addressed: no pathway in the corpus sets a GPA.

question: Is there a rule about how long an applicant has to complete a license application after starting it?

answer.reference_answer: The LICN policies do not set a deadline for completing a license application after it is started, and they do not say when an incomplete application expires. They do define when an application counts as complete: the applicant must submit all information and credentials required by the License Application policy, pay the application fee, and, if applicable, be cleared from any Superintendent investigation. Separately, a complete application for a licensure service other than renewal must reach DPI by April 15 of a fiscal year to guarantee processing before that fiscal year ends, and a later complete application not approved before year end bars the employing unit from using State or federal funds for the applicant's salary that year. That April 15 date is a processing deadline, not a deadline to finish an application. For any incomplete-application rule outside this corpus, the analyst should check with the DPI Licensure Section.

key_points.point: The policies do not set a time limit for an applicant to finish an application after starting it, and they do not state when an incomplete application expires.

An application is complete only when the applicant has submitted all required information, documentation, and credentials, paid the application fee, and, if applicable, been cleared from any Superintendent investigation.
Required application contents are listed in the License Application policy, and the application fee is set by the Licensure Fees schedule.

A complete application for a licensure service other than renewal must be submitted to DPI by April 15 of a fiscal year to guarantee processing before that fiscal year ends. A complete application submitted after April 15 that DPI does not approve before fiscal year end means the employing unit cannot use State or federal funds for the applicant's salary for that fiscal year. This is a processing deadline, not a deadline to complete an application.

out_of_scope_parts: Any time limit for completing an application after it is started, and any rule that an incomplete application expires or is closed.
answer.reviewer_notes: The corpus is silent on completion or abandonment deadlines for applications, so the correct verdict is not_covered. The April 15 rule in LICN-001 §3(f) is the closest provision and could be mistaken for a completion deadline; the reference answer clarifies that it is a processing deadline for complete applications. LICN-007 §3(d) gives a 60-day window to contest a proposed order, which applies to disciplinary and denial proceedings, not to application completion, so it should not be cited here. Also note that the April 15 rule excludes renewal applications.

question: What's the difference between a lateral entry license and a traditional license in NC?

answer.reference_answer: The adopted policies do not define a current 'lateral entry license' or a 'traditional license' as license types. The term 'lateral entry' appears only in references to former lateral entry licenses issued under G.S. 115C-297, a statute the policies say was repealed by S.L. 2017-189, and those holders may move to a residency license or limited license under the conditions stated in the policies. The current license classifications are the initial professional license, continuing professional license, residency license, limited license, permit to teach, emergency license, international faculty license, lifetime license, and provisional license. The policies do not use the word 'traditional'; the closest match is an IPL or CPL based on completion of a North Carolina educator preparation program, which the policies require for a teacher license. The corpus cannot say how the former lateral entry license was treated before its repeal.

key_points.point: The term 'lateral entry license' is not a current license classification in the adopted policy series; it appears only in references to former licenses issued under G.S. 115C-297, which the policies state was repealed by S.L. 2017-189.

A person who previously held a former lateral entry license and did not convert it before expiration may qualify for a residency license in the same area if they meet G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5) and have passed the applicable licensure examination for that content area.

A former lateral entry license holder who has not passed the licensure examination but otherwise meets IPL or CPL requirements may qualify for a limited license if currently employed by the PSU and the PSU submits the required affidavit.

The policies do not define a 'traditional license.' The nearest concept is an IPL or CPL based on completing a recognized North Carolina educator preparation program and EPP recommendation, which is a general requirement for a teacher license.

For applicants who have not completed an EPP, the current policies provide other license pathways, including a residency license (requested by a PSU), an emergency license, a permit to teach, and a limited license, each with its own conditions.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the analyst asking about a specific educator who previously held a lateral entry license, or about a new applicant?
Did the educator complete a North Carolina educator preparation program, and did they pass the applicable licensure examination?
Which license area and license classification is the educator currently holding or seeking?
false_premises: The question assumes 'lateral entry license' is a current NC license type alongside a 'traditional license.' The adopted policies do not list a lateral entry license as a current classification. They mention only former lateral entry licenses issued under G.S. 115C-297, which the policies say was repealed by S.L. 2017-189.
The question assumes 'traditional license' is an official license name. The policies do not use this term.
out_of_scope_parts: The policies do not describe how lateral entry licenses were issued, what their requirements were, or how they differed from other licenses before the statute was repealed. The corpus cannot confirm the pre-repeal rules.
Repealed statute G.S. 115C-297 is not included in the corpus.
answer.reviewer_notes: The policies never define 'lateral entry' or 'traditional' as terms. The answer relies on the two passages that mention former lateral entry licenses (LICN-019 §1(c) and LICN-023 §1(b)). Mapping 'traditional' to an IPL or CPL earned through an EPP is my interpretation, not policy language, so it is presented as the nearest match only. The corpus does not confirm the rules that applied before the repeal. An assistant that says lateral entry is a current license type would be wrong.

question: Does NC require background checks before issuing any educator license, and what does it cover?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not use the term background check or describe a DPI-run fingerprint or records check. Every applicant for a professional educator license must submit a statement and documentation disclosing any prior license suspension or revocation in North Carolina or another state, and any criminal history not previously expunged, including pending or dismissed charges, unfulfilled deferred prosecution agreements, and convictions (guilty pleas, no contest pleas, and guilty verdicts). An application is complete, and DPI issues the license, only after the applicant has been cleared of any Superintendent investigation that applies to them, and the Superintendent may investigate from any source and must consider the applicant's disclosures. A conviction can be grounds to deny a license, but the Superintendent weighs factors such as the relationship to professional duties, severity, and remorse, and the policies do not say how records are checked or how renewals are handled.

key_points.point: Every applicant for a professional educator license must complete an application that includes a statement and supporting documentation disclosing any prior suspension or revocation of a professional license in NC or any other state.

The required criminal history disclosure covers any criminal history not previously expunged, including pending or dismissed charges, deferred prosecution agreements whose terms are not yet fulfilled, and convictions.
Conviction is defined broadly to include a guilty plea, a no contest or nolo contendere plea, and a guilty verdict or finding by a jury, judge, or other adjudicatory body.

DPI issues the license only after the application is complete. For applicants, completeness includes being cleared from any investigation the Superintendent conducted under LICN-007, if applicable. The policies do not say when such an investigation is triggered.
The Superintendent investigates allegations or information from any source and must consider information the license applicant disclosed in the application.

The Superintendent may deny a license application for a criminal conviction in any state, federal, or territorial court, if a preponderance of the evidence supports it, and must weigh factors including the relationship to professional duties, severity, impact on students, culpability, remorse, reform, and likelihood of future misconduct. Fraud or material misrepresentation in the application is a separate denial ground.

A separate criminal history reporting duty applies to PSU administrators and charter boards for employees, under G.S. 115C-332(e) as governed by LICN-007. That duty is employer-side reporting and is not a DPI licensing precondition.

The policies do not describe how DPI checks criminal records (for example fingerprinting or which databases are used), a separate check deadline, or how renewal applicants' criminal history is handled.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is this an initial application or a renewal? The policies do not clearly address criminal history disclosure or investigation clearance for renewals.
Which license classification and license area is sought?
Does the applicant have any criminal history, including pending, dismissed, deferred, or convicted charges (and whether any record was expunged)?
Is there any open Superintendent investigation, or any prior license suspension or revocation in North Carolina or another state?
Did the applicant disclose all of the required information on the application?
false_premises: The policies do not use the term background check or require a DPI-run background check for all educator licenses. The requirement is applicant self-disclosure of criminal and license history, plus clearance of any applicable Superintendent investigation before the application is complete.
out_of_scope_parts: How DPI actually conducts any criminal records check, including fingerprinting, databases, vendors, and turnaround time.
Background check or criminal history treatment for license renewal applications.
The text of G.S. 115C-332(e), which is cited by LICN-007 §9(g) but is not in the corpus.
Whether a particular record qualifies as expunged under Chapter 15A, Article 5, which is referenced but not in the corpus.
answer.reviewer_notes: No policy uses the phrase background check. The answer maps the question onto applicant disclosure in LICN-004 §1(h) and investigation clearance in LICN-001 §3(e)(iii). LICN-001 §3(e)(iii) says 'if applicable' and does not say when an investigation is triggered, so describing clearance as required before issuance applies only where an investigation exists. LICN-004 §1 applies to 'any applicant for professional educator license', which supports 'any license' for initial applications. LICN-007 §9(g) concerns employer-side criminal history reporting and cites G.S. 115C-332(e), which is not in the corpus; it is included so the analyst does not confuse it with the DPI licensing requirement. Confidence is medium because it is unclear whether DPI runs its own check and how renewals are handled.

question: Can a licensed teacher hold two different NC licenses at the same time, like a classroom license and a school services license?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not expressly say whether one educator may hold a teacher license and a student services personnel license at the same time. They establish three license classifications (Teacher, Administrator, Student Services Personnel) and require each professional educator employed in a public school unit to hold, or be qualified to hold, a license. The only add-on mechanism addresses adding teaching license areas to an existing IPL or CPL, not adding a separate student services classification. A student services license requires a master's or higher educator preparation program, and a teacher license is limited to the highest degree level completed, but the policies do not say how these combine for one person. The analyst should confirm the specific license types and levels with the DPI Licensure Section before advising.

key_points.point: The policies define three license classifications (Teacher, Administrator, Student Services Personnel) and require any professional educator employed in a North Carolina public school to hold, or be qualified to hold, a professional educator license for that role. They do not expressly address whether one person may hold licenses from two classifications at the same time.

The add-on rule permits an applicant to add a new license area to an existing IPL or CPL, but it applies to teaching license areas. Teaching areas may be added only after meeting the examination requirements or completing 24 credit hours, and some areas (Elementary Education, Exceptional Children: General Curriculum) can be added only by exam. This is an add-on within the teaching license, not a separate student services license.

A student services personnel license requires a master's, specialist, or doctoral educator preparation program, and a teacher license is limited to the highest degree level at which the applicant completed a program. These degree rules govern eligibility for each license separately; the policies do not say whether they permit or bar holding both at once.

Where the policies restrict combinations, the restrictions concern the same license area (for example, a residency license holder cannot receive a permit to teach or emergency license in the same area, and a permit applicant must never have held any other North Carolina professional educator license). These do not settle whether different classifications may be held concurrently.

missing_facts_to_ask: Which specific licenses are involved (for example, which teacher license area and which student services classification such as school counselor or school psychologist)?
What is the educator's highest degree and the level of the educator preparation program completed, since degree level limits each license?
Is the educator currently holding an IPL or CPL, and is either license a residency, permit, or emergency license?
Is the educator employed in both roles, or is the second license being sought for a different position?
false_premises: The terms 'classroom license' and 'school services license' are not policy titles. The corpus uses Teacher license (LICN-010) and Student Services Personnel license (LICN-012).
out_of_scope_parts: Whether a single educator may hold a teacher license and a student services personnel license concurrently is not addressed by any policy in the corpus.
How salary, experience credit, or pay is affected by holding two licenses is not addressed in the policies provided.
answer.reviewer_notes: The corpus is silent on concurrent holding of different license classifications. The verdict is not_covered and the answer relies on related rules, not a direct statement. The only add-on mechanism (LICN-013) is limited to teaching license areas and does not address student services classifications. The term 'classroom license' is not a policy term. The degree-level rules in LICN-010 §3 and LICN-012 §3 may constrain eligibility, but the corpus does not say they bar concurrent holding. No outside knowledge was used. Reviewer should confirm that no other LICN policy (outside the corpus) addresses dual classifications before the answer is given to the analyst.

question: Where can I find the official NCDPI policy number for CPL renewal requirements?

answer.reference_answer: The policy that governs renewal of a teacher's continuing professional license (CPL) is LICN-030, License Renewal for Teachers, which requires renewal every five years and sets the CEU requirements. If the license holder is an administrator, the governing policy is LICN-031, and for student services personnel it is LICN-032. LICN-033 holds the general renewal rules that apply to all CPLs. LICN-024 covers how a CPL is obtained rather than how it is renewed. The policy text does not say where these policies are published, so the analyst will need to confirm the official location, such as the DPI or State Board of Education policy pages, outside this corpus.

key_points.point: For a teacher's CPL, the renewal requirements are in LICN-030, which requires renewal every five years and CEU requirements for each renewal cycle.
Administrator CPL renewal is governed by LICN-031, and student services personnel CPL renewal is governed by LICN-032.
General renewal rules for all CPLs, including CEU sources, National Board certification credit, and PSU responsibilities, are in LICN-033.
LICN-024 is the policy for obtaining a CPL (qualifications), not renewing one. A renewal cycle is the five-year period between CPL renewals.
The corpus does not state where these policies are published officially, so it cannot confirm the DPI web location or any official policy number beyond the LICN identifiers.

question: Teacher has a CPL expiring in 3 months and has 6.5 CEUs from this cycle, 1.0 of them in digital learning. Enough to renew?

answer.reference_answer: No, not as stated. A teacher renewing a CPL needs eight CEUs per five-year renewal cycle, and 6.5 CEUs leaves a shortfall of 1.5 CEUs (15 clock hours, or 1.0 semester credit hour). The category breakdown also matters. Grades PreK-5 need 3 CEUs in the license area, 3 in literacy and 2 general. Grades 6-12 need 4 in the license area and 4 general. The 1.0 digital learning CEU can only count toward a category it fits (most likely the general CEUs, if germane to K-12), and the policies do not define digital learning as its own category. To give a final answer on categories, the analyst needs the grade band and how the other 5.5 CEUs break down. The teacher also needs a most recent annual evaluation of at least proficient, as defined in the policy, if employed by a local board of education. Only National Board Certification earned this cycle (credit for all eight CEUs) or the General Assembly member exemption would change the total shortfall.

key_points.point: A CPL must be renewed every five years, and a teacher needs eight CEUs per renewal cycle. 6.5 CEUs is below eight regardless of category mix.
For Pre-K through Grade 5 the eight CEUs must be 3 in the license area (Standards 3 and 4), 3 on literacy and 2 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment.
For Grades 6 through 12 the eight CEUs must be 4 in the license area (Standards 3 and 4) and 4 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment.

The 1.0 digital learning CEU can only count if it fits a required category. The policies do not name digital learning as a category, so it would count as a general CEU if germane to K-12, or as a license-area CEU if it meets Standards 3 and 4. Each PSU must set procedures for deciding whether an activity is appropriate for the educator.
CEUs can be earned through college credit or professional development programs. One CEU is 2/3 of a semester credit hour or 10 clock hours, which defines how the remaining 1.5 CEUs could be earned.
Mandatory training hours count toward CEUs only if the educator has otherwise met the renewal requirements. They cannot be used to fill the gap on their own.

Separate from CEUs, a teacher employed by a local board must have a most recent annual NCEES evaluation of at least proficient (Proficient or higher on three of five standards, including Standard 4). If the teacher is in the final year of the cycle and was not proficient, the LSAU may use a mandatory improvement plan, which leads to an IPL.

Exceptions that would change the CEU total: National Board Certification earned this cycle gives credit for all eight CEUs. A General Assembly member serving during the cycle is exempt if they notify DPI.

missing_facts_to_ask: What grade band does the teacher serve (Pre-K-5 or 6-12)? This determines the category breakdown.
How are the other 5.5 CEUs distributed across license-area, literacy and general categories?
Does the digital learning CEU relate to the teacher's license area or is it general K-12 professional development?
Does the teacher hold or expect to receive National Board Certification (or renewal of it) this cycle?
What was the teacher's most recent annual NCEES evaluation rating?
Is the teacher employed by a local board of education?
Are any of the 6.5 CEUs from mandatory training hours?
out_of_scope_parts: Whether digital learning qualifies as license-area or general CEUs is not defined in the policies. It depends on the PSU's appropriateness determination and Standards 3 and 4 alignment.
answer.computation: Required: 8 CEUs. Earned: 6.5 CEUs. Shortfall = 8 - 6.5 = 1.5 CEUs. Using the CEU definition (1 CEU = 10 clock hours or 2/3 semester credit hour): 1.5 x 10 = 15 clock hours, or 1.5 x 2/3 = 1.0 semester credit hour. Category check: Pre-K-5 requires 3 + 3 + 2 = 8. Grades 6-12 requires 4 + 4 = 8. The 1.0 digital learning CEU could fill at most part of one category.
answer.reviewer_notes: The total CEU count (6.5 < 8) answers the question regardless of grade band, so the verdict is no. The category breakdown cannot be fully checked without the grade band and the breakdown of the other CEUs. I treated digital learning as most plausibly a general CEU, but the policies do not say so, so this is an interpretation. The 3-month timing is not directly relevant because the policies set no CEU timing rule. Licenses expire June 30. A late renewal fee appears in LICN-008, but that policy is dated 2018 and was not used.

question: cpl renewal short 2 credits what now

answer.reference_answer: A teacher holding a CPL must complete 8 CEUs in each five-year renewal cycle, divided by grade band, so a shortfall of 2 CEUs leaves the renewal requirement unmet. The policies do not state a specific consequence for a CEU shortfall at the deadline. The only policy path that addresses a teacher who does not renew is the mandatory improvement plan, which is tied to the evaluation rating rather than to CEU totals, and it results in an IPL only if the teacher otherwise meets licensure requirements. Before advising, confirm whether the license is teacher, administrator, or student services, the grade band, which category is short, whether the teacher is employed and rated proficient, and whether any mandatory training hours or other qualifying activities are unclaimed, since those can count toward CEUs. Any late-renewal fee or extension is not tied to CEU shortfalls in the policies and should be confirmed with DPI.

key_points.point: A teacher renewing a CPL must complete 8 CEUs during each five-year renewal cycle, with the mix set by grade band (K-5 or 6-12). A shortfall of 2 means the CEU requirement is not met.

The required mix matters for diagnosing the gap. For K-5 teachers, 3 CEUs must be in the license area, 3 must be literacy-related, and 2 must be general. For 6-12 teachers, 4 must be in the license area and 4 must be general. The 2-CEU gap could fall in any of these categories, and the policies do not say how a category shortfall is treated.

CEUs can come from college credit or professional development. One CEU is either two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours of professional development. Hours from mandatory training required by state law or by the local board can count toward CEUs if the educator has otherwise met the renewal requirements.

The teacher must also have a rating of at least proficient on the most recent annual evaluation to renew a CPL, and this is a separate requirement from the CEU count. The mandatory improvement plan route applies to a teacher in the final year of a cycle who was not rated proficient. If placed on a plan and otherwise eligible, the teacher receives an IPL with a term of 60 or 90 instructional days depending on the school's status. The policies do not say whether a CEU shortfall alone qualifies for this route.

Under the policies, a license expires on June 30 of its expiration year unless renewed. The text of LICN-030 §2(b)(iv) on expiration is ambiguous, as it refers to a teacher who meets the Section 1 criteria but is not placed on a mandatory improvement plan. If it applies to a CEU shortfall, the license expires at the end of the cycle, and the teacher may apply for an IPL 30 days after receiving notice of expiration.

The policies do not state a grace period, extension, or waiver for CEUs that are short at the renewal deadline. The fee table lists a late renewal fee of $35 and a school-system renewal window of April 15 through July 31, but it does not connect these to CEU shortfalls. That table dates from 2018.
If the license is an administrator or student services license, the rule is different: 8 CEUs with a 4-4 split (leadership or discipline-aligned, plus general), not the K-5 or 6-12 teacher mix.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the license a teacher license, an administrator license, or a student services personnel license? The renewal rules differ by type.
For a teacher, what is the grade band (Pre-K through 5, or 6 through 12)? The required CEU mix depends on it.
Which required category is short by 2 CEUs (license area, literacy, general, or another)?
Is the teacher currently employed by a local board of education, and what was the most recent annual evaluation rating?
Is this the final year of the five-year renewal cycle, and has the local school administrative unit placed the teacher on a mandatory improvement plan?
How many CEUs has the teacher already completed in this cycle, and are any unclaimed mandatory training hours or National Board credits available?
Is the 'deadline' the June 30 expiration date, or the end of the April 15 to July 31 renewal window?
Is the 2-credit shortfall measured in CEUs or in semester credit hours? The policies use CEUs.
false_premises: The question implies the policies set a specific outcome for a CEU shortfall at the deadline. The policies do not state one for a shortfall of CEUs.
The question uses 'credits' for the renewal requirement, but the policies measure renewal in CEUs (continuing education units).
out_of_scope_parts: Whether DPI would grant an extension, waiver, or grace period for a short CEU count is not addressed in the policies.
The literacy CEU content standard in G.S. 115C-270.30(b)(2) is cited by LICN-030 but the statute is not in the corpus.
Local school administrative unit continuing education rules beyond the state requirements, which LICN-033 §5(b) allows, are not in the corpus.
Beginning Teacher Support Program requirements (TCED-016) are not in the corpus and are not part of the CEU question.
Whether the late renewal fee applies in this situation is not stated in the policies; the fee table is dated 2018.
answer.computation: Teacher CPL renewal requires 8 CEUs per five-year cycle (LICN-030 §1). If the 2-CEU shortfall is measured against the full 8, the teacher has earned 6 of 8. Each CEU is either two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours (LICN-001 §2(g)), so 2 CEUs equal 4/3 (about 1.33) semester credit hours or 20 clock hours of professional development. If the shortfall falls in one category (for example, 3 literacy CEUs for K-5 or 4 general CEUs for 6-12), the category minimum still applies.
answer.reviewer_notes: The policies do not address a CEU shortfall at the renewal deadline. The only consequence provisions are the mandatory improvement plan (LICN-030 §2(b)), which is tied to the evaluation rating, and the expiration clause in LICN-030 §2(b)(iv). The expiration clause refers to a teacher who 'meets the criteria in Section 1' but is not placed on a plan, which appears garbled or inverted, so I did not treat it as a clear rule for CEU shortfalls. LICN-030 §1(a)(ii) cites G.S. 115C-270.30(b)(2), which is not in the corpus. The LICN-008 fee table is dated 2018 and its renewal window (April 15 to July 31) does not clearly match the June 30 expiration in LICN-001 §3(g). The analyst's question omits the license type, grade band, and total credits, so the answer is conditional and needs the missing facts before any advice is given.

question: Candidate's Initial Professional License expires June 30. They have 14 renewal credits for the cycle, and 3 of them are from a graduate course in exceptional children. Does that count toward the requirement?

answer.reference_answer: An Initial Professional License is a three-year nonrenewable license, so the 14-credit renewal cycle does not apply to it as described. Renewal rules apply to a Continuing Professional License, and an IPL moves to a CPL by meeting the conversion requirements, which do not include CEUs unless the IPL was issued under a mandatory improvement plan. Once renewal applies, a teacher needs eight CEUs per cycle, with a category split that depends on grade band: grades PreK-5 need three license-area, three literacy, and two general CEUs, while grades 6-12 need four license-area and four general CEUs. One CEU equals two-thirds of a semester credit hour, so a 3-semester-hour graduate course is 4.5 CEUs, and it counts toward the license-area requirement only if the teacher's license area is Exceptional Children. The analyst needs to confirm the grade band, license area, whether the 14 credits are semester hours or CEUs, and whether the IPL was issued under a mandatory improvement plan before answering.

key_points.point: An IPL is a three-year nonrenewable license, so it is not renewed with a 14-credit cycle as the question assumes.
Renewal every five years with CEU requirements applies to a Continuing Professional License; an IPL converts to a CPL by meeting the LICN-024 requirements, which do not list CEUs.
Exception: if the IPL was issued under a mandatory improvement plan, completion of the required CEUs is a condition of applying for the CPL at the end of the three-year IPL term.
A CEU is two-thirds of a semester credit hour from an institution of higher education or ten clock hours of professional development; 3 semester hours equals 4.5 CEUs.
Eight CEUs per cycle are required. For PreK-5 teachers: three license-area, three literacy, and two general CEUs. For grades 6-12 teachers: four license-area and four general CEUs.

Whether the graduate Exceptional Children course counts toward the license-area category depends on whether the teacher's license area is Exceptional Children (General Curriculum is one listed EC area). Otherwise it can only count toward general CEUs if germane to K-12, which the policy does not explicitly address for this course.
The policies do not contain a separate Exceptional Children renewal requirement; the Exceptional Children question turns on license area and category.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the candidate's license area Exceptional Children, or is it a different area such as a grade-level or content area?
What grade band does the candidate teach (PreK-5 or 6-12), and is the candidate a teacher rather than an administrator or student services personnel?
Are the 14 credits semester credit hours or already-converted CEUs? If semester hours, the 3-hour course equals 4.5 CEUs.
Was the IPL issued under a mandatory improvement plan (LICN-030 §2(b))? If so, CEUs are required for conversion to a CPL.
Is the candidate converting an IPL to a CPL, or is the candidate holding a CPL that is up for renewal? Which activity does the June 30 expiration refer to?
Does the candidate have three years of licensed teaching experience and a completed Beginning Teacher Support Program, and have the licensure exam requirements been met?
Did the 14 credits fall within the current renewal cycle, and do they come from qualifying sources (college credit or professional development programs)?
false_premises: The IPL is treated as a renewable license with a renewal cycle and 14 renewal credits; LICN-001 §2(k) defines the IPL as a three-year nonrenewable license, and renewal rules apply to a CPL.
The question implies a single exceptional children requirement; the policies set general CEU categories by grade band and do not impose a separate Exceptional Children requirement.
out_of_scope_parts: The policies do not say whether a graduate course is treated differently from other college credit for CEUs; they define CEUs by semester-hour equivalence only.
The policies do not address whether one course can satisfy both the license-area and general CEU categories at once.
answer.computation: 3 semester credit hours / (2/3 semester hour per CEU) = 4.5 CEUs (LICN-001 §2(g)(i)). If the 14 credits are semester hours: 14 / (2/3) = 21 CEUs, which exceeds the 8-CEU total. If the 14 credits are already CEUs: 14 CEUs, which also exceeds 8. Total count is therefore not the constraint; the category split is. The 2-CEU course can contribute at most 2 toward a category: for grades 6-12, the 4 license-area CEUs (if the license area is Exceptional Children) or 4 general CEUs; for PreK-5, the 3 license-area CEUs or 2 general CEUs.
answer.reviewer_notes: The draft's premise that an IPL is renewed is contradicted by LICN-001 §2(k), so the answer corrects the premise and then explains the CPL path. Several facts are missing that decide the outcome: grade band, license area, whether 14 and 3 are semester hours or CEUs, and whether the IPL came from a mandatory improvement plan. The policy does not explicitly say whether a graduate EC course counts as general CEUs, nor whether one course can satisfy two categories. The question says 'the requirement' in the singular, but the policy sets several category requirements. The corpus has no explicit provision about EC-specific CEUs.

question: teacher with RL, 2 yrs in, renewing? 8 CEUs

answer.reference_answer: The 8 CEUs do not count toward renewing a Residency License. Renewal of a residency license is not based on a CEU count. The employing public school unit must document to DPI that the teacher is enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program, is employed as a teacher in that unit, acquired at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completed the 10 days of professional development required in the first year of the license. The CEU requirement of eight CEUs per five-year cycle applies to renewing a continuing professional license, not a residency license. Whether this teacher can renew depends on those four documented items, which the question does not provide. The residency license is a one-year license renewable twice, and if the teacher does not satisfy the requirements by June 30 of the third year, it must convert to an IPL or CPL, which requires the EPP's recommendation and the IPL or CPL requirements.

key_points.point: A Residency License is a one-year license renewable twice, so the teacher is in the middle of the allowed residency term.

Residency license renewal is governed by LICN-019 §2(a), which requires the employing PSU to document four conditions to DPI: enrollment in a recognized EPP, employment as a teacher in the PSU, at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year, and completion of 10 days of professional development in the first year of the license. CEUs are not one of the listed conditions.

The eight-CEU renewal requirement (four in the license area and four general for grades 6-12, or the Pre-K-5 variant) applies to teachers renewing a continuing professional license every five years. The question's CPL-style count does not apply to a residency license.

The 10 days of professional development required under the residency license are defined by LICN-019 §5 and are not satisfied by CEUs as the policies are written. The PSU must provide the required training, which may be split with five days in preservice and five days in the first year.

The residency license must be converted to an IPL or CPL by June 30 of the third year of the residency license, and conversion requires meeting IPL or CPL requirements and the EPP's recommendation. If the requirements are not met by that date, the residency license expires and the IPL or CPL takes effect when the requirements are met.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the teacher enrolled in a recognized educator preparation program?
Is the teacher currently employed as a teacher by the same public school unit or eligible nonpublic school that requested the residency license?
Did the teacher acquire at least six months of teaching experience during the preceding school year?
Did the teacher complete the 10 days of professional development required in the first year of the residency license, and how was it delivered (preservice, first year, or split)?
Which year of the residency license is the teacher entering for this renewal (second or third), and has the license already been renewed once?
Is the 8 CEUs the analyst mentioned the teacher's own record, and is there a separate CPL in the teacher's history that might be the source of the CEU count?
false_premises: The question assumes a residency license is renewed using a CEU count, as a CPL is. The policies require PSU documentation of enrollment, employment, six months of teaching experience, and first-year professional development instead. CEUs are not part of residency license renewal.
out_of_scope_parts: The policies do not say whether CEUs earned by a residency license holder may count toward the 10-day professional development requirement in LICN-019 §5. That question is not answered and the analyst should not assume they do.
answer.reviewer_notes: The question is terse and ambiguous: 'renewing?' could mean the renewal for the second year or the conversion at year three. The reference answer addresses both by stating the renewal documentation and the June 30 third-year conversion deadline. The policy text for LICN-019 §2(a)(iv) requires the 10 days of PD to be completed 'in the first year of the residency license,' which may matter if the teacher is at the start of year two. LICN-019 §2(a) says the PSU must provide the documentation, so the analyst should confirm the PSU is the one submitting. The policy text for LICN-019 §5(d) contains an internal cross-reference error ('Subsections (2)(d)(ii) through (2)(d)(v)') that does not affect this answer. The reviewer should confirm the drafter's intent that the 8 CEUs relate to a CPL, since the question may have been drafted assuming a CPL-style count.

question: A CPL holder finished a 3-credit graduate course in school counseling last spring. Does that course count toward renewal if the holder is a classroom teacher and not a counselor?

answer.reference_answer: The course cannot count toward the teacher's license-area CEUs, which must be earned in the teacher's own license area consistent with Standards 3 and 4; school counseling is a separate student services classification. It could count toward the general CEU category only if it is germane to the K-12 educational environment, and the employing PSU must consider whether it is directly related to the teacher's work responsibilities before recommending it. Under the policy's CEU definition, 3 semester credit hours equal 4.5 CEUs (3 divided by 2/3), which would exceed the 4 general CEUs required for grades 6-12 but cannot fill the license-area requirement. The policies do not say whether excess CEUs can be applied to another category or whether the course must fall within the current renewal cycle, so those points need confirmation from DPI.

key_points.point: The course cannot satisfy the teacher's license-area CEU requirement. Teachers must earn a set number of CEUs in their teacher license area consistent with Standards 3 and 4, and school counseling is a separate student services license classification, so a counseling course is not in the teacher's license area unless that is the teacher's license area.

The course may be eligible for the general CEU category. Teachers must also earn general CEUs that are germane to the K-12 educational environment, and the policies use that K-12 standard rather than a match to the individual's specific role. The policies do not define 'germane,' so whether a counseling course meets it is an interpretation.

The employing PSU controls whether the course is recommended. When determining whether an activity is appropriate for renewal credit, the PSU must consider the direct relationship between the activity and the educator's work responsibilities, and PSUs may add their own continuing education requirements. For a classroom teacher, a counseling course is therefore at risk of being rejected at the PSU level even if it meets the K-12 standard.

Credit conversion: one CEU equals two-thirds of a semester credit hour from an institution of higher education, so a 3-semester-hour course equals 4.5 CEUs. That is more than the 4 general CEUs required for grades 6-12, but the course cannot be used for the license-area CEUs, so the full renewal requirement of 8 CEUs still needs other activities.

The policies are silent on whether CEUs in excess of one category's requirement may be applied to another category, and on whether a course taken last spring falls within the current renewal cycle. The renewal policy refers to 'each renewal cycle' but does not define cycle dates or carry-over rules.

missing_facts_to_ask: Which grade band the teacher teaches (Pre-K through Grade 5 or Grades 6 through 12), because the category totals differ.
Whether the teacher's license area is anything related to school counseling (the question implies it is not).
Whether the 3 credits are semester credit hours, since the CEU conversion depends on that.
Whether the course was taken from an institution of higher education.
Whether the course falls within the teacher's current renewal cycle.
Whether the employing PSU has reviewed the course and found it directly related to the teacher's work responsibilities.
How many CEUs the teacher has already earned in each category this cycle.
false_premises: The premise that relevance to the licensed role determines credit eligibility is only partly correct. The license-area CEU requirement is tied to the teacher's license area, and the PSU must consider the relationship to work responsibilities, but the general CEU category is judged by whether the activity is germane to the K-12 environment, not by a match to the individual's role.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether the course would count toward other requirements such as the teacher's evaluation or mandatory improvement plan (LICN-030 §2), which are separate from CEU counting.
Salary or graduate pay effects of the course (LICN-006), which the question does not ask about.
answer.computation: Under LICN-001 §2(g)(i), one CEU = 2/3 semester credit hour, so 3 semester credit hours ÷ (2/3) = 4.5 CEUs. Grades 6-12 requires 4 general CEUs, so 4.5 CEUs could satisfy that category if the course is accepted as general credit, but it cannot be counted toward the 4 license-area CEUs. Grades Pre-K-5 requires 2 general CEUs, with separate 3-CEU license-area and 3-CEU literacy categories that this course cannot fill.
answer.reviewer_notes: Interpretation required: the policies do not define 'germane to the K-12 educational environment,' so whether a school counseling course qualifies for the general category is a judgment call. The question's 'relevance to the licensed role' framing is only partly supported by the text. The question says '3-credit' but the CEU conversion is defined for semester credit hours, so the 4.5 figure assumes semester hours. The policies do not say whether excess CEUs can be applied to another category, or whether a course taken last spring falls in the current renewal cycle, and the corpus cannot confirm cycle dates. The grade band (K-5 versus 6-12) is not given and changes the category totals, though the license-area conclusion holds for either band.

question: Teacher's Emergency License runs out at the end of the school year. They have completed 9 of the 12 semester hours required for a standard license. Can the Emergency License be extended?

answer.reference_answer: No. Under LICN-018, an Emergency License is valid only until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested and cannot be extended or renewed, so it cannot be extended past the end of the year. The policies do not set a 12-semester-hour requirement for a standard license, so the 9 of 12 figure cannot be measured against a policy threshold. The hours counted toward a residency license are different: residency requires at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or a passed licensure exam, so 9 hours alone would not qualify. If the teacher has passed the applicable exam, a PSU could request a residency license, but only if the teacher also meets the statutory requirement cited in LICN-019 and is not barred by LICN-018.

key_points.point: An Emergency License cannot be extended or renewed. It is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested.
An Emergency License is a one-year nonrenewable license, so the teacher cannot keep it for another year through renewal.

Licenses expire on June 30 of the calendar year in which they are set to expire unless renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy. Because the EL cannot be extended or renewed, it expires on June 30 and cannot run past the end of the school year.
The policies do not contain a 12-semester-hour requirement for a standard license, so the 9 of 12 hours cannot be checked against a policy threshold.

Hours in a content area matter for residency: an applicant may qualify for a residency license with at least 24 hours of coursework in the content area or by passing the applicable licensure exam. An EL holder is not eligible for residency if the applicant qualifies for residency, and the EL cannot be used once residency is available.
Hours toward adding a teaching area on an existing IPL or CPL use a 24-credit-hour standard with a grade of C or better, which is a different path from the EL.

missing_facts_to_ask: Has the teacher passed the applicable licensure exam for the content area?
How many hours of coursework does the teacher have in the content area for the license sought, and is it 24 or more?
What exact standard license is meant (IPL, CPL, or another type)? The policies do not define a standard license.
Which fiscal year was the Emergency License requested for, and has the teacher already held a residency license in this area?
Where does the 12-semester-hour figure come from (PSU policy, a different license, or an employer requirement)? It is not in the LICN corpus.
false_premises: The 12 semester hours required for a standard license do not appear in the LICN policies.

The Emergency License expires at the end of the school year. The policy says it is valid until June 30 of the fiscal year for which it was requested, which may not match the school year end date exactly.
out_of_scope_parts: The 12-semester-hour requirement for a standard license is not in the corpus, so the policies cannot say whether 9 of 12 hours is enough.
Hours or course requirements for any state statute cited in LICN-019 (G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5)) are not in the corpus.
Requirements for the specific standard license type are not set out in the policies provided.
answer.computation: Arithmetic only: 12 minus 9 leaves 3 semester hours remaining, but the 12-hour threshold is not in the LICN policies, so this figure is not a policy-based result. Residency under LICN-019 uses a 24-hour threshold, which would leave 15 hours (24 minus 9) if the teacher had no passed exam.
answer.reviewer_notes: The extension answer is clear: LICN-018 §3 says the EL cannot be extended or renewed. The main gap is the 12-semester-hour figure, which does not appear in the corpus; the analyst should confirm its source. The draft type renewal_math was relabeled as eligibility because no renewal arithmetic applies to an EL. The policy's June 30 expiration may differ from a school-year end date, so the answer uses the policy text. LICN-018 §1(c) links the EL to the residency pathway, so if the teacher passed the exam, the residency question needs its own check against G.S. 115C-270.20(a)(5), which is not in the corpus.

question: Applicant's license lapsed 14 months ago. They have 0 renewal credits on record since it lapsed. What's the reinstatement math?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not contain a reinstatement calculation for a lapsed license. The reinstatement language in LICN-007 §8 applies only to revoked licenses or denied applications, and no rule converts a 14-month lapse into a credit requirement. The closest pathway is validation of an expired continuing professional license under LICN-033 §3, which a public school unit may request for an educator under its employment even without the requisite CEUs, provided the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year. A validated CPL is effective for three years, and the educator must complete the renewal requirements for their license type by the end of that third year to renew for a new five-year cycle. The 0 renewal credits matter because a full renewal requires 8 CEUs per cycle for teachers, administrators, or student services personnel. The answer depends on the license type, whether it was a CPL, the exact expiration date, and the educator's PSU employment history, so the analyst should not assume a license type.

key_points.point: The policies contain no reinstatement calculation for a lapsed license. The reinstatement and reconsideration process in LICN-007 §8 applies only to a license that was revoked or an application that was denied, and it requires waiting 12 months before petitioning.

The only policy route for an expired CPL without the requisite CEUs is validation. A PSU governing body may request validation for an educator under its employment, even without the requisite CEUs, but only if the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year.

A validated CPL is effective for three years. The educator must complete the relevant renewal requirements (LICN-030, LICN-031, or LICN-032) by the end of the third year to renew the CPL for a new five-year cycle.

Renewal requires 8 CEUs per cycle. For a teacher in Pre-K through Grade 5 the 8 CEUs are 3 in license area, 3 literacy, and 2 general; for a teacher in Grades 6 through 12 they are 4 in license area and 4 general. For an administrator they are 4 leadership and 4 general, and for student services personnel 4 standards-aligned and 4 general. Zero credits on record means all 8 are outstanding for a full renewal.
Under the CEU definition, one CEU is either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from a higher education institution or ten clock hours of professional development.
Licenses expire on June 30 of the year set for expiration unless renewed, extended, or converted, so the exact expiration date should be confirmed before any timing analysis.

For a teacher whose license expired at the end of a renewal cycle without a mandatory improvement plan, the teacher may apply for an IPL 30 days after receiving the DPI notice of expiration. This applies only to a teacher who met the Section 1 criteria and was not placed on a plan by the employing LSAU.
Teacher renewal also requires evidence of a rating of at least proficient on the most recent annual evaluation for teachers employed by a local board of education.

The fee for validating an expired CPL, when the request is opened by the employing school system, is $60 in the fee schedule. That schedule is dated 2018 and should be checked against the current amount.

missing_facts_to_ask: What type of license lapsed: teacher, administrator, or student services personnel, and whether it was a CPL, IPL, or another type (validation under LICN-033 §3 applies only to an expired CPL)?
What is the exact expiration date of the license (licenses expire June 30 under LICN-001 §3(g), and 14 months ago should be reconciled with that date)?
Has the educator been employed by any North Carolina PSU since the license expired, and if so, in which fiscal years?
Was the license ever revoked, or was an application denied? If so, LICN-007 §8 applies and the 12-month waiting period matters.
Will the employing PSU governing body request validation on the educator's behalf?
Does the educator hold National Board certification, which affects CEU credit under LICN-033 §2?
Is the educator a member of the General Assembly, which may exempt them under LICN-030 §3?
false_premises: That the policies define a reinstatement calculation for a lapsed license. The reinstatement process in LICN-007 §8 applies only to revoked licenses or denied applications.
That renewal credits earned since the lapse determine reinstatement. Validation under LICN-033 §3 may proceed even without the requisite CEUs.
out_of_scope_parts: Any late-renewal eligibility rule or time limit for renewing a lapsed license. The corpus lists a Late Renewal fee in LICN-008 but contains no policy text defining when late renewal is allowed.
Any definition of a lapsed license as distinct from an expired one. The corpus does not define lapse.
Any reinstatement timeline for a lapsed (rather than revoked) license.
answer.computation: Full renewal requires 8 CEUs per cycle, so with 0 credits on record all 8 are outstanding. Under LICN-001 §2(g), one CEU is two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours, so 8 CEUs equal 8 x 2/3 = 5.33 semester credit hours from a higher education institution, or 8 x 10 = 80 clock hours of professional development. The 14-month lapse does not reduce this count, since the corpus contains no time-based reduction. Validation under LICN-033 §3 does not itself require the CEUs, but the validated CPL must be renewed within three years by completing the applicable requirements.
answer.reviewer_notes: The draft is labeled renewal_math, but the policies contain no arithmetic for lapsed-license reinstatement; I relabeled it missing_facts. The term reinstatement in the question does not match the corpus usage. The corpus does not define lapse, and the 14-month figure is not tied to any policy deadline. Relative to the snapshot date of 2026-10-10, 14 months before is about August 2025, which does not match a June 30 expiration under LICN-001 §3(g); the exact date should be confirmed. The phrase preceding fiscal year in LICN-033 §3 is not anchored to a specific date, so its application depends on when validation is requested. LICN-008 is dated 2018, so the $60 validation fee may be outdated. The LICN-030 renewal requirements are teacher-specific and the admin and SSP CEU counts are taken from LICN-031 and LICN-032. The license type is unknown, so no single rule should be assumed.

question: Teacher has 30 CEUs but the cycle only counts hours earned after the last renewal date. 12 of the 30 were earned before that date. How many count?

answer.reference_answer: Under the policies, CEUs count toward a teacher's renewal only if earned during the current renewal cycle, which is the five-year period between renewals of the CPL. The 12 CEUs earned before the last renewal date fall outside that cycle, so 18 of the 30 CEUs count. The policies require eight CEUs per cycle for teachers in any grade band, so 18 exceeds the total requirement. Whether the 18 satisfy the required breakdown depends on the teacher's grade band and how the CEUs are categorized, which the question does not give. The policies also measure CEUs rather than hours, and the question does not say whether the 30 figure is in CEUs.

key_points.point: A renewal cycle is the five-year period between each renewal of a CPL, so CEUs earned before the last renewal date fall outside the current cycle and do not count toward it.
Teachers holding a CPL must complete eight CEUs during each renewal cycle, so only CEUs earned within the cycle count toward that requirement.
Arithmetic: 30 total minus 12 earned before the last renewal date leaves 18 CEUs within the cycle. That exceeds the eight-CEU requirement, but the required breakdown by category still has to be met.

The requirement is eight CEUs in either grade band, but the split differs: grades Pre-K to 5 need three license-area, three literacy, and two general CEUs; grades 6 to 12 need four license-area and four general CEUs. The category split of the 18 CEUs is therefore needed to confirm compliance.
A CEU is defined as either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from a higher education institution or ten clock hours of professional development, so the unit of count is CEUs rather than raw hours.
The policies do not address whether CEUs in excess of the requirement (here 10) carry forward to a later cycle.

missing_facts_to_ask: What grade band does the teacher teach (Pre-K through 5, or 6 through 12)?
How many of the 18 in-cycle CEUs fall into each category: license area, literacy (for K-5), and general?
What is the exact date of the teacher's last CPL renewal, and were all 18 CEUs earned on or after that date?
Does the teacher currently hold a CPL, as opposed to an IPL or residency license?
Is the 30 figure in CEUs, or in semester or clock hours that need converting under the CEU definition?
Were any of the CEUs National Board credit (LICN-033 §2) or mandatory training hours (LICN-033 §4)?
false_premises: The policies do not use the phrase 'earned after the last renewal date' or describe a date-window rule in those words; the date limit follows from the definition of renewal cycle and the 'during each renewal cycle' requirement.
The question refers to counting 'hours'; the policies count CEUs, so the unit should be CEUs.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether the 12 earlier CEUs were valid for a prior renewal cycle.
Whether CEUs in excess of the eight-CEU requirement carry over to the next cycle.
Whether the employer approved the activities for renewal credit beyond the PSU criteria in LICN-033 §5.
answer.computation: 30 total CEUs minus 12 CEUs earned before the last renewal date = 18 CEUs within the current renewal cycle. Required total is 8 CEUs under LICN-030 §1 (either grade band). 18 is more than 8, so the total requirement is met. The category breakdown (license area, literacy, general) is not known and must be checked separately.
answer.reviewer_notes: The count of 18 is the main answer. The date-window rule is inferred from the definition of renewal cycle in LICN-001 §2(v) (the five-year period between each CPL renewal) combined with LICN-030 §1's requirement to complete CEUs 'during each renewal cycle.' The policies never state that CEUs before the last renewal date are excluded in those words, so the reviewer should confirm that this reading matches the analyst's intent. The question says 'hours,' but the policies count CEUs, so I treated the 30 as CEUs. Grade band and category split are needed before confirming full compliance. The policies in the corpus do not explain carryover of excess CEUs.

question: cpl 4 years 11 months in, credits?

answer.reference_answer: For a teacher holding a CPL, the policies require 8 CEUs during each five-year renewal cycle, and the split depends on grade band. Teachers in Pre-K through Grade 5 need 3 CEUs in the license area, 3 literacy CEUs, and 2 general CEUs; teachers in Grades 6 through 12 need 4 license-area CEUs and 4 general CEUs. One CEU is either two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours, so 8 CEUs equals about 5.33 semester hours or 80 clock hours. The policies do not give the exact expiration date for this license, but with about one month left in the cycle the teacher must complete the CEUs or the license expires at the end of the cycle unless the employing LSAU places a teacher on a mandatory improvement plan. Administrators and student services personnel have different CEU breakdowns, so the role and grade band need to be confirmed before giving a final figure.

key_points.point: A CPL teacher must renew every five years and complete 8 CEUs during each renewal cycle.
Grades Pre-K through 5 teacher breakdown: 3 CEUs in the license area, 3 CEUs related to literacy, and 2 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment.
Grades 6 through 12 teacher breakdown: 4 CEUs in the license area and 4 general CEUs germane to the K-12 environment.

A CEU is either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from an institution of higher education or ten clock hours of professional development programming. The policies use CEUs, not credits, for renewal.

A renewal cycle is the five-year period between each renewal of a CPL. The policies do not state the exact cycle start or end date for this educator, so the remaining time cannot be fixed from the facts given.

If the teacher is employed by an LSAU and was not rated proficient on the most recent evaluation, the LSAU may place the teacher on a mandatory improvement plan in the final year of the cycle. Otherwise the license expires at the end of the renewal cycle.
Licenses expire June 30 of the calendar year in which they are set to expire unless renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy.

Ways CEUs can be earned include college or university credit and professional development programs. Mandatory training counts toward CEUs only if it is required by State law or by the local board and the educator has otherwise met the renewal requirements. National Board certification earns full credit for the cycle in which it is received.

If the educator is an administrator or student services personnel rather than a teacher, the requirement is also 8 CEUs per cycle but with a different split (administrators: 4 leadership-focused and 4 general; student services: 4 aligned to EVAL standards and 4 general).

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the educator a teacher, an administrator, or student services personnel? The question says only CPL.
If a teacher, what grade band (Pre-K through 5 or 6 through 12) is the license area?
Is the educator employed by a local school administrative unit, and what was the most recent annual evaluation rating?
What is the exact date the current renewal cycle began and the date the CPL expires?
Has the educator already earned any CEUs this cycle, and in what categories (license area, literacy, general, National Board, mandatory training)?
Is the educator a member of the General Assembly during this cycle, which would trigger the exemption?
out_of_scope_parts: The exact expiration date of this license, since the policies do not give the cycle start date for an individual educator.
Whether a late renewal would be allowed, and the associated fee, beyond the general late renewal fee listed in the fee schedule.
Whether any specific course or activity qualifies as a CEU in a particular category, beyond the general criteria.
answer.computation: Definition from LICN-001 §2(g): 1 CEU = 2/3 semester credit hour OR 10 clock hours. Total required = 8 CEUs. In semester hours: 8 x 2/3 = 5.33 semester credit hours. In clock hours: 8 x 10 = 80 clock hours. Band split for Pre-K through 5: 3 license-area + 3 literacy + 2 general = 8. Band split for 6 through 12: 4 license-area + 4 general = 8. Time: 4 years 11 months = 59 months of a 60-month cycle, so about 1 month remains. This is approximate because the policies do not define the start date precisely.
answer.reviewer_notes: The question says only CPL and 'credits.' The policies use CEUs, not credits, and the answer changes by role (teacher vs. administrator vs. student services) and grade band, so the verdict is needs_more_info. The draft note about 'deadline timing' does not map to a specific deadline in the corpus: the cycle is five years and expiration falls June 30 of the year set under LICN-001 §3(g), but the corpus does not state the cycle start or expiration date for an individual.
