The policies provide no reinstatement procedure for an expired Permit to Teach. The reinstatement provisions cover revoked licenses or denied applications (LICN-007 §8), residency licenses that the employing PSU failed to renew (LICN-019 §2(b)), and expired CPLs that a PSU asks DPI to validate (LICN-033 §3); none applies to a permit.

A new permit may be requested by a PSU governing body only if the applicant holds at least a bachelor's degree and has never been issued any other North Carolina professional educator license. Whether the earlier permit counts as an other license is not stated, so the analyst should confirm this with the Licensure Section.

Intervening licensure matters. A person who holds or previously held a residency license cannot receive a permit or emergency license in the same area, and an emergency license is available only to a person who does not qualify for a residency license.

missing_facts_to_ask: The exact expiration date on the permit, and the fiscal year it was requested for. Under the policy the permit expires June 30, so an expiration two months before the October 10, 2026 snapshot would not match a June 30 date.

Whether the person has ever been issued any North Carolina professional educator license other than this permit, including an initial professional, continuing professional, residency, emergency, or limited license.
Whether the person holds at least a bachelor's degree.
Whether the person is currently employed by a PSU that wants to request a new permit, and whether a permit is the license being sought or whether another license type is.
Whether the person has held a residency license in the same license area, since that bars a permit and an emergency license there.
false_premises: The question assumes an expired Permit to Teach can be reinstated. The policies provide no reinstatement route for a permit, which cannot be renewed or extended after it expires.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether DPI would exercise discretion or grant an exception for a lapsed permit, since the policies set no such exception.
Salary or State Salary Schedule consequences of the lapse, beyond the permit's pay-level rule that applies only while a permit is held.
Any application fee for a new permit, since LICN-008 lists no permit-specific fee.
answer.reviewer_notes: Read this first. The policies do not provide reinstatement for an expired Permit to Teach, and the verdict is needs_more_info because a new permit depends on licensing history the question does not give. The reading of LICN-017 §1(b) is an interpretation: it is unclear whether a previously issued permit counts as any other North Carolina professional educator license. The analyst should check with the Licensure Section. The stated timing also looks inconsistent: a permit expires June 30, and 2 months before 2026-10-10 is August 10, 2026, so the exact expiration date should be confirmed.

question: Candidate has an MLS from a university, applying for NC media coordinator. Is that enough?

answer.reference_answer: An MLS alone does not settle eligibility. Media coordinator is a student services personnel classification that requires completion of an educator preparation program at the master's level or higher, and the EPP must be recognized by the SBE or the equivalent licensing authority where it is based. The policies key on EPP completion and recognition, not on program accreditation. The candidate must also satisfy the media coordinator licensure exam (Praxis 5312, required score 154) before or during the third year of licensure, with at least one attempt in the first year. Whether the candidate gets a CPL or an IPL depends on whether the exam was already passed before application. The analyst needs to confirm whether the MLS came through a recognized EPP and the candidate's exam status.

key_points.point: Media coordinator is a student services personnel classification, so the student services personnel license rules apply.

Student services personnel licensure requires completion of an educator preparation program at the master's level or higher. A degree alone is not the stated test, so the MLS must have been earned through an EPP.
The EPP must be recognized by the SBE or the equivalent licensing authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business.
The applicant's documentation must include official transcripts for the degree and an EPP official's signed verification that the applicant completed an EPP for the license classification sought.
The media coordinator licensure exam is Praxis 5312 with a required score of 154. Exam status is needed to determine eligibility and license type.

The applicant must satisfy the exam before or during the third year of licensure and must attempt it at least once in the first year. Passing before initial application leads to a CPL; otherwise the applicant receives an IPL.

Program accreditation is not stated as a licensure gate for student services personnel. The accredited-institution condition appears only in the graduate pay provisions of LICN-006, which concern salary and not licensure.

missing_facts_to_ask: Was the MLS earned through an educator preparation program (EPP), and is that EPP recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent licensing authority where the EPP is based?
Is the MLS program at the master's level, and does the EPP official's signed verification confirm completion of an EPP for the media coordinator classification?
Has the candidate already passed the Praxis 5312 (media coordinator, required score 154)? If so, when? If not, has the candidate attempted it, and when will it be attempted?
Does the candidate already hold any North Carolina professional educator license, and what kind?
Does the candidate hold a clear license from another state, and how many years of licensed experience does the candidate have?
Is the candidate applying for a new license, a conversion, or a renewal?
false_premises: The draft notes say program accreditation is the key gate for media licensure. The policies do not make accreditation the gate. They require completion of an EPP recognized by the SBE or the equivalent licensing authority (LICN-001 §3(d); LICN-012 §3), and accreditation appears only in the graduate salary provisions of LICN-006 §V(a).
answer.reviewer_notes: The question does not say whether the MLS came through an EPP, so the answer turns on that fact. The draft's accreditation premise is not supported by the policy text. The corpus has no rule that treats an MLS alone as qualifying for media coordinator. LICN-025's out-of-state provisions are written mainly for teacher license areas (LICN-025 §2(b)(ii) refers to LICN-010), so applying them to an out-of-state media coordinator candidate is an interpretation. The LICN-003 table row for Media Coordinator (code 076, Praxis 5312, score 154) is a rendered table and was read as shown. The corpus holds only current versions and cannot confirm earlier requirements.

question: Teacher on a limited license for a special subject, 3 years in. Can they keep renewing it?

answer.reference_answer: A limited license is a three-year renewable license for a teaching area, so renewal is possible only if the conditions in LICN-023 are met. The employing PSU must submit a renewal affidavit, signed by the supervising principal and the local superintendent, confirming the teacher is currently employed by that PSU, is an effective teacher, and that the PSU will encourage a CPL pursuit. The teacher must also meet or exceed expected EVAAS growth where data is available, measured as an average over the years since the license was first issued or last renewed, with 2019-2020 and 2020-2021 excluded. The limited license cannot be transferred to another PSU, except for servicemembers and spouses under LICN-028. The policies do not state a cap on the number of renewals or a deadline for passing the licensure exam, so the analyst should confirm those points with DPI.

key_points.point: A limited license is a three-year renewable license for teachers who completed an EPP but have not satisfied the licensure exam requirements, so renewal is structurally allowed.

Renewal requires the employing PSU to submit an affidavit, signed by the supervising principal and local superintendent, attesting the licensee is currently employed by the PSU, is an effective teacher, and that the PSU will encourage pursuit of a CPL.

Renewal also requires the licensee to meet or exceed expected EVAAS growth where data is available; with more than one year of data, DPI averages the growth data, limited to years since the license was first issued or last renewed, and excludes 2019-2020 and 2020-2021.

The limited license is tied to the PSU that employs the teacher and cannot be transferred to another PSU, except for servicemembers and spouses covered by LICN-028; LICN-028 §6 lets a servicemember's limited license remain valid after a within-North Carolina move under military orders.

The special subject must be a teaching license area, which is what the limited license covers; limited licenses are not issued for administrator or student services areas. Special Subjects are a listed teaching classification, and EVAAS growth data availability may depend on the subject taught.
The limited license cannot have additional license areas added to it, so any added subject would need a different route.
The policies do not state a maximum number of limited license renewals or a deadline for the teacher to pass the licensure exam while on a limited license; the answer should not assume one.

missing_facts_to_ask: Is the teacher currently employed by the same PSU that holds the limited license, and has the teacher moved to another PSU?
Will the principal and local superintendent sign the renewal affidavit confirming effectiveness and encouragement to pursue a CPL?
Which special subject is the teaching area, and is EVAAS growth data available for it?
How many years of EVAAS growth data exist since the license was first issued or last renewed, and did the teacher meet or exceed expected growth?
Was the limited license issued under the lateral entry conversion path (LICN-023 §1(b)) or the PSU request path (LICN-023 §1(a))?
Has the teacher passed any required licensure exam since the limited license was issued, which could allow a CPL or IPL instead?
Is the teacher a servicemember or spouse relocating under military orders?
Does 3 years in mean three years since first issuance, or the end of the current three-year term?
out_of_scope_parts: Whether the policies set a maximum number of limited license renewals (not addressed in the corpus)
Whether there is a deadline for passing the licensure exam while holding a limited license (not addressed in the corpus)
answer.reviewer_notes: The draft note says renewal depends on employer request and subject. The policies support the employer affidavit requirement, but subject matters only indirectly: a special subject must be a teaching area, and EVAAS data availability may vary by subject, while the policy text does not make renewal depend on subject category. The question's phrase 3 years in is ambiguous; the policies describe a three-year term, not a three-year count of time in service. The corpus has no cap on renewals and no exam deadline for limited license holders beyond the general framework, so the answer flags these as gaps rather than inferring them. LICN-023 §1(b)(ii) refers to the principal of the applicant's school while §2(a) refers to the supervising principal; both are treated as the same role.

question: International applicant, bachelor's from India, 6 years teaching math there, wants NC license. Next steps?

answer.reference_answer: Because the bachelor's and teaching experience come from India, the applicant is an out-of-state applicant, and a foreign country counts as a jurisdiction. With about six years of teaching, the applicant does not fit the out-of-state initial professional license route, which is limited to fewer than three years of licensed experience. The likely route is a continuing professional license under the out-of-state rules, which requires a current clear license from India or another jurisdiction, plus either National Board certification or licensure requirements substantially similar to North Carolina's (a recognized educator preparation program and a passing exam score for each license area), with exam results presented at initial licensure. The outcome depends on whether the six years were licensed teaching, whether the bachelor's came from a recognized teacher preparation program, whether a valid Indian license is held, whether an exam was passed, and the grade band (which sets the math license area). Next steps are to gather the facts above and assemble a complete application (transcripts, EPP documentation, license proof, background disclosure, fee), submitted by April 15 to be processed before the fiscal year ends. The policies do not describe a credential evaluation process for foreign degrees, so that step must be confirmed outside this corpus.

key_points.point: The applicant is an out-of-state applicant because the policies define that term to include international preparation programs, and a foreign country is a jurisdiction.

The out-of-state initial professional license route applies only to applicants with fewer than three years of licensed professional educator experience, so six years of teaching does not fit that route on its face.

Applicants with more than three years of licensed experience may qualify for a continuing professional license if they hold a clear license from another jurisdiction and meet either the National Board certification option or the substantially-similar option, which requires an educator preparation program recognized by the state where it is located and a passing score on an out-of-state exam for each license area sought.

A clear license must be in good standing, renewable by the issuing authority, free of discipline and pending unprofessional-conduct investigations, and not voluntarily surrendered under investigation. Whether an Indian license meets this must be confirmed.

Out-of-state exam results must be presented at initial licensure, and an out-of-state applicant may not use out-of-state exam results to convert an initial professional license to a continuing professional license.

A teacher license requires completion of an educator preparation program at a listed degree level, and the applicant is eligible only at the highest degree level at which an EPP was completed. A bachelor's degree alone is not shown to be an EPP completion, so the nature of the Indian degree matters. EPPs must be recognized by the SBE or the equivalent licensing authority where the program is based.

The license area depends on the grade band taught: Middle Grades Mathematics (grades 6-9) or Secondary Mathematics (grades 9-12). North Carolina's required mathematics tests differ by band, which matters if no qualifying out-of-state exam score is available.

The application must include the required components, including official transcripts, EPP documentation, a background disclosure, proof of any current license from another state if applicable, and documentation of exam performance, along with the applicable fee. The out-of-state initial professional license fee is listed as $100. A complete application is required before the license is issued.

A complete application for a licensure service (other than renewal) must reach DPI by April 15 to guarantee processing before the fiscal year ends. A later application that DPI does not approve before fiscal year end cannot be paid from State or federal funds for that year.
If the applicant holds a J-1 visa and does not qualify for any other DPI license, an international faculty license may be an option, but it requires sponsor approval and is not renewable.

The policies do not describe a credential evaluation service or process for judging whether an Indian degree or teacher preparation is equivalent to a North Carolina program, and they do not say how teaching experience in India is credited for salary.

answer.computation: Threshold comparison: six years of teaching is greater than three years. The IPL route under LICN-025 §1(a) requires fewer than three years of licensed experience (6 is not less than 3), so it does not apply. The CPL route under LICN-025 §2 applies to more than three years (6 is greater than 3), but only if all six years were licensed professional educator experience.

question: RL teacher, passed Praxis, 2 yrs in. Upgrade to IPL?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not make a passed Praxis score the trigger for converting a residency license to an IPL. Conversion requires meeting the LICN-020 IPL requirements and a recommendation from the educator preparation program (EPP) that prepared the licensee. Under LICN-020, the applicant must have completed a recognized NC EPP and been recommended by it, completed an out-of-state EPP, or hold an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of licensed experience. The two years matter mainly for timing: if the requirements are met by June 30 of the residency license's third year, the IPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year; otherwise it is effective when the requirements are met. The passed exam matters for a later CPL, not for this IPL conversion. Whether this teacher qualifies depends on facts the question does not give, especially the EPP recommendation and the current status of the residency license.

key_points.point: The question is about converting a residency license to an IPL. The policies govern this as a conversion requiring that the IPL requirements in LICN-020 be met and that the EPP that prepared the licensee recommend the conversion.
The EPP recommendation is a stated requirement for converting a residency license. The question does not say whether the teacher has one, so this is a key missing fact.

The IPL requirements in LICN-020 are alternatives: completion of a recognized NC EPP with EPP recommendation, completion of an out-of-state EPP, or an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of licensed experience. Which applies depends on the teacher's preparation and out-of-state history, which the question does not give.

Passing the Praxis is not listed as a prerequisite for an IPL in LICN-020. LICN-020 §2 also contemplates an IPL being issued where exam requirements are not yet satisfied. The exam requirement appears in the CPL rule, so a passed exam is relevant to a later CPL conversion rather than this IPL.

Timing: if the conversion requirements are met by June 30 of the residency license's third year, the IPL is effective July 1 of the next fiscal year. If not, the residency license expires and the IPL is effective on the date the requirements are met. Two years in places the teacher in year two, so the deadline is still ahead, but the policies do not give the license's start date.

Renewal of the residency license in year two requires documentation that the teacher is enrolled in a recognized EPP, is employed as a teacher in the PSU, acquired at least six months of teaching experience in the prior school year, and completed 10 days of professional development in the first year. The question does not say whether these were met, so it is unclear whether the residency license is still in effect.

missing_facts_to_ask: Did the teacher complete a recognized North Carolina EPP, an out-of-state EPP, or hold an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of licensed experience?
Has the EPP that prepared the teacher recommended the conversion to an IPL?

The corpus does not address how the two years of teaching count toward salary experience credit.
answer.reviewer_notes: The policies conflict on whether an EPP recommendation is needed: LICN-020 §2 says that for a PSU-requested IPL, EPP recommendation is not required when exams are unmet, but LICN-019 §3(a)(ii) requires EPP recommendation for residency-to-IPL conversion. I treated the residency-specific rule in LICN-019 §3 as controlling because it is more specific. question: Teacher has a CPL in science and wants to add math 6-9. How many credits?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not tie the add-on requirement to the teacher's existing math preparation. A CPL holder may add Middle Grades (6-9) Mathematics either by passing the Middle Grades Mathematics licensure exam (Praxis 5164, required score 157) or by completing 24 credit hours of coursework from an institution of higher education in the mathematics area with a grade of C or better in each course. Only the coursework route requires credits, so the answer is 24 credit hours, or zero if the exam is passed instead. Mathematics is not one of the areas that must be added by exam only, so the coursework option is available. CEUs are not used for add-ons, so the 24 credit hours should not be converted to CEUs.

key_points.point: A CPL holder may add a new teaching license area either by satisfying the licensure examination requirements for that area or by completing 24 credit hours of higher-education coursework in the area with a grade of C or better in each course.
For Middle Grades (6-9) Mathematics, the required test is Praxis 5164 with a required score of 157, so passing that exam means no coursework credits are needed.

Mathematics is not among the areas (Elementary Education and Exceptional Children: General Curriculum) that can be added only by examination, so the 24-credit-hour coursework route is open for this add-on.
The policy sets a fixed 24-credit-hour figure for the coursework route and does not reduce it based on prior math preparation.
The fee schedule has an add-on row titled Add Area by Test or 24 Sem. Hrs. at $60, which suggests the 24 hours are semester hours.

CEUs are defined for license renewal (one CEU equals two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours), so they do not measure add-on coursework and should not be used to count the 24 credit hours.

missing_facts_to_ask: Will the teacher add the area by passing the Middle Grades Mathematics exam or by completing coursework? The credit count depends entirely on this choice.
If coursework: has the teacher already completed any college mathematics courses with a grade of C or better, and would those count toward the 24 hours? The policy does not address prior coursework.
If coursework: are the credits from an institution of higher education and are they semester hours? The policy text says only credit hours.
Is the CPL in good standing and does the teacher hold no other North Carolina license that would change the add-on process?
false_premises: The draft note says the credit requirement depends on existing math preparation. The add-on rule in LICN-013 sets 24 credit hours for the coursework route regardless of prior preparation, and the exam route involves no credits.
out_of_scope_parts: Which specific courses qualify as being in the mathematics license area, and whether prior coursework counts toward the 24 hours, are not defined in the policies.
Whether the science CPL's own license area (for example, Middle Grades Science or Secondary Science) affects eligibility is not addressed beyond the general add-on rule.
Any requirement that a teacher on a CPL complete the Beginning Teacher Support Program does not apply to an add-on and is not addressed in the add-on policy.
answer.computation: Coursework route: 24 credit hours from an institution of higher education, each course at grade C or better (LICN-013 §1(b)). Exam route: 0 credits, pass Praxis 5164 with a score of 157 (LICN-003 §5). No CEU conversion is applied, because the CEU definition (2/3 semester credit hour) belongs to renewal credit (LICN-001 §2(g)(i)).
answer.reviewer_notes: LICN-013 says credit hours without specifying semester or quarter. The fee table row Add Area by Test or 24 Sem. Hrs. (LICN-008) suggests semester hours, but this is an inference and should be flagged. The draft note about existing math preparation is not supported by the policy text. The question's wording suggests a coursework route, but the exam route is equally valid and needs no credits. LICN-013 §1's restriction on adding areas to an IPL before exam completion does not apply because the teacher holds a CPL.

question: What's the current salary step for a teacher with a CPL and 12 years experience at Union County?

answer.reference_answer: The licensure policies in the corpus do not contain the State Salary Schedule or any step amounts, so the current salary step cannot be determined from them. They do explain how creditable experience is counted for salary purposes: a full-time school year of at least six calendar months earns one year, part-time work requires at least 15 hours per week, partial years can be combined, and substitute, tutor, and clerical service does not count as professional educator experience. Whether 12 years produces a given step depends on the employment record, which the analyst must verify, and the step itself must be taken from the State Salary Schedule. The CPL does not change experience credit under these policies, and the corpus does not address local Union County pay.

key_points.point: The corpus does not contain the State Salary Schedule values or step placements, so the current salary step cannot be stated from the policies. The schedule is defined only by reference to its statutory administration.
Salary is determined by the amount of creditable experience. Experience credit requires full-time work of at least six calendar months within a fiscal year (July 1 through June 30) to earn one year.
Part-time work counts only if it is at least 15 hours per week, and partial years of full-time or part-time service can be combined into experience credit.

Service as a tutor, clerical paraprofessional, or substitute teacher is not recognized as professional educator experience credit, and no credit is awarded during an approved leave of absence (except as required by workers' compensation and USERRA). The 12 years must be checked against these exclusions.

The policies do not tie experience credit or salary placement to holding a CPL. The CPL is a license classification, and the policies place only permit, emergency, and international faculty licensees at the A-level with zero years of experience for salary purposes.

Degree level affects salary only through the highest degree from an EPP, and graduate salary pay requires separate criteria under LICN-006 Section V. The corpus does not say whether the teacher holds a graduate degree or qualifies for graduate pay.
The policies do not address Union County Public Schools' local pay practices or any local salary supplement.

Does the teacher hold a graduate degree or qualify for graduate salary pay under LICN-006 Section V?
What State Salary Schedule table or step document is the analyst using? That source is outside this corpus.

question: how long does DPI take to process a license application after its submitted online

answer.reference_answer: The licensure policies do not state how long DPI takes to process a license application, and they do not address online submission. DPI issues a license once the application is complete. Completeness requires submitting all information and credentials required by LICN-004, paying the application fee under LICN-008, and, if applicable, being cleared from any Superintendent investigation under LICN-007.

The only timing guarantee is an April 15 cutoff for complete applications (other than renewals) to be processed before the end of the fiscal year. A complete application submitted after April 15 is not guaranteed processing that fiscal year, and the employing public school unit may not use State or federal funds to pay the applicant's salary for that fiscal year if DPI does not approve the application by then.

question: A candidate's Praxis score came back 2 points under the cutoff. Does the testing vendor allow a score review or rescore, and how much does it cost?

answer.reference_answer: The LICN policies do not say whether the testing vendor allows a score review or rescore, and they set no cost for one. question: Teacher wants to know if Union County will pay for their master's program tuition if they stay 3 more years.

answer.reference_answer: The licensure policies do not address whether Union County Public Schools pays master's tuition, and tuition reimbursement is a district funding decision outside this policy series. The policies do address a related but different benefit: graduate degree salary authorization on the State Salary Schedule, which the district may recommend to DPI if the degree is from an accredited institution, is directly related to the educator's license area or assignment, and meets the assignment-time requirement. key_points.point: The policies do not say whether a district pays or reimburses tuition for a master's program, and no licensure rule ties tuition payment to a commitment to stay employed for a set number of years.

Graduate degree salary authorization is a separate benefit. DPI authorizes pay at the master's level for educators with a qualifying master's degree, and a PSU may recommend the educator for it. It is not a tuition payment.

question: A teacher with 15 years in a private school in Florida wants to know how much the district will pay them on the step schedule if they're hired here.

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not give a dollar amount or step placement, because the State Salary Schedule values are not in the corpus and the district's pay decision falls outside the licensure series. LICN-006 does govern how years of experience are credited for salary: one year per full-time job of at least six calendar months in a school unit during a fiscal year, with part-time work requiring at least 15 hours per week and partial years combinable. Private school experience is not clearly addressed; the only explicit exclusion is one-teacher private schools, so whether 15 years there count depends on whether the schools were multi-teacher, the work was full-time, and the work was teaching rather than non-teaching. Non-teaching experience counts only if the hiring LEA recommends it, the work was relevant and at least half-time, and DPI accepts it. The analyst should confirm the job type, hours, school structure, and any Florida or other licenses held before estimating credit.

key_points.point: The policies do not provide a dollar amount or step placement. The State Salary Schedule is administered by the SBE under G.S. 115C-12, but no schedule values appear in the corpus.

Salary for a NC public school employee is set by creditable experience. One year of credit is earned for full-time work of at least six calendar months in a school unit within one fiscal year (July 1 through June 30).

Part-time work counts only with at least 15 hours per week, and it earns a year only if it totals six full-time calendar months in a fiscal year. Partial years of full-time or part-time work can be combined.

Private school experience is not addressed by a general credit rule. The only explicit exclusion is experience in a one-teacher private school. The policy does not define 'school unit' or say whether multi-teacher private schools or out-of-state private schools count, so the answer depends on facts about the school.
Tutor, clerical paraprofessional, and substitute service is not credited as professional educator experience, and leave of absence time is not credited.

If the Florida work was non-teaching, it may count only on the recommendation of the hiring LEA and only if it was at least half-time (20 hours or more per week), completed after age 18, not on-the-job training, paid and documented, and found directly related to the license area by DPI.
Non-teaching credit is 1 year for every 2 full-time years completed before the bachelor's degree and 1 year for every full-time year completed after it.
A license lists the holder's years of professional experience and highest degree level, so the NC license issued will carry the experience figure DPI accepted.

Out-of-state licensed experience affects license type: an out-of-state applicant with fewer than three years of licensed experience may qualify for an IPL, and more than three years may qualify for a CPL. Only licensed experience counts for these thresholds, so unlicensed private school years do not clearly affect them.
If DPI rejects the LEA's recommendation for non-teaching or graduate credit, the LEA may appeal to the Superintendent.

answer.computation: Credit counts by fiscal year. Teaching work earns at most one year of credit per fiscal year, so 15 years could yield at most 15 years of credit only if every year was full-time, at least six calendar months, in a qualifying school unit (not a one-teacher private school). Partial years combine: for example, two part-time years equal to six full-time months count as one year. If the work was non-teaching and relevant, each full year before the bachelor's degree earns one-half year (15 years would yield at most 7.5 years, and the policy does not say how fractions are rounded), while each full year after the bachelor's degree earns one full year (15 years would yield at most 15).
answer.reviewer_notes: Policy numbering defects in LICN-006: the non-teaching credit ratio and criteria appear under an unlabeled paragraph after a section labeled §II, and two sections are labeled §IV (military leadership and recommendations/appeal). The appeal is cited as §IV(a), which is a sub-item of the second §IV. The policy does not define 'school unit' and does not say whether multi-teacher private schools count, so the private school point is an interpretation; the one-teacher exclusion suggests multi-teacher private schools may be considered, but the text does not say so. The corpus does not contain the State Salary Schedule, so no dollar or step answer is given. The draft's 'unanswerable' label is wrong for the experience-credit portion. LICN-006 is the current adopted version (effective 2025-07-01); the corpus cannot confirm what applied earlier.

question: This international applicant has a foreign teaching degree and needs a work visa. Will UCPS HR sponsor the H-1B visa, and how long does it take?

answer.reference_answer: The licensure policies do not say whether UCPS HR will sponsor an H-1B visa or how long visa processing takes, so that part cannot be answered from the corpus. The only visa-linked licensing rule is the International Faculty License, which applies to foreign nationals holding a J-1 visa who meet no other DPI license requirement, requires a DPI-approved sponsor, and is issued only at the sponsor's request. For the foreign teaching degree, the policies require that the educator preparation program be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent authority where the program is based, and the applicant must submit official transcripts and proof of EPP completion. The applicable initial license depends on the applicant's out-of-state credentials and years of licensed experience, and the April 15 application deadline affects salary funding if missed. The analyst should refer the visa sponsorship and timing questions to UCPS HR and federal immigration sources.

key_points.point: The policies do not address whether UCPS HR sponsors an H-1B visa, who makes that decision, or how long federal work visa processing takes.

The only licensing provision tied to a visa is the International Faculty License, which covers foreign nationals holding a J-1 cultural exchange visa who do not meet the requirements for any other DPI license.

A J-1 applicant also needs a sponsor approved by DPI, and the license is issued only at the sponsor's request. It cannot be renewed but may be extended for two years with the sponsor and PSU's request while the J-1 visa remains active.

A foreign-trained applicant is treated as an out-of-state applicant, and the EPP must be recognized by the SBE or by the equivalent authority in the jurisdiction where the EPP has its principal place of business.

Out-of-state applicants with fewer than three years of licensed experience may qualify for an IPL by completing an EPP based outside North Carolina or by holding a clear license from another jurisdiction. Elementary and Special Education: General Curriculum require the NC exam by the end of the third year. Other areas require either an out-of-state exam pass or the NC exam, and the NC exam must be attempted in the first year.

A teaching license is available only at the highest degree level completed through an EPP, and the application requires official transcripts, proof of EPP completion, and documentation of any licensure exam performance.
An out-of-state initial professional license application carries a fee of $100 under the fee schedule.

A complete licensure application for a non-renewal service submitted after April 15 may not be approved before fiscal year end, and then the employing PSU may not use State or federal funds to pay the applicant's salary for that fiscal year.

question: Teacher got a nonrenewal notice from UCPS in April. What's the deadline to file a grievance with the district?

answer.reference_answer: The LICN policies do not set a deadline for a grievance with the district, and they do not describe a district grievance process. Any grievance timeline would come from UCPS or board policy and the employment contract, which are not in this corpus, so the analyst should check those documents. The 60-day window in LICN-007 applies only to a licensure proposed order from the Superintendent, and the 30-day notice in LICN-007 applies to resignations, so neither should be used for a grievance. Separately, LICN-007 sets reporting duties for the employing PSU's administrators after a nonrenewal: 5 calendar days if the underlying conduct is misconduct as defined in the policy, or 30 calendar days if the conduct may otherwise justify sanctions, with the educator to be notified of the reporting requirement at separation. Whether either duty applies depends on the nonrenewal date and reason, which the question does not give.

key_points.point: The policies do not address a district grievance process or any grievance filing deadline; that timeline would come from local board policy or the employment contract, which are outside the corpus.

The 60-day deadline in LICN-007 concerns commencing an administrative proceeding under Chapter 150B to contest a Superintendent's proposed licensure order. It is not a grievance deadline and should not be applied here.
The 30-day notice in LICN-007 for resignations without notice is a separate provision about separation and is not a grievance deadline.

A nonrenewal of the employment contract can trigger a reporting duty for a PSU administrator. If the conduct is misconduct as defined in the policy, the report is due in writing to the Superintendent within five calendar days of the nonrenewal.
If the nonrenewal is for conduct that does not meet the misconduct definition but may justify sanctions, the administrator must report within 30 calendar days of the nonrenewal.
The PSU must notify the educator of the reporting requirement upon separation from employment when a report may be required.
The policies do not say that an employment nonrenewal by itself changes the CPL. License renewal rules govern license status and do not address employment nonrenewal.

Whether the teacher has been or will be the subject of any investigation or complaint.
The UCPS grievance policy or the employment contract, which would set any grievance deadline.
Whether the teacher is seeking a grievance or is asking only about licensure consequences.
false_premises: That a grievance deadline with the district is governed by the licensure policies. The corpus does not address district grievances; the drafter's note that the timeline comes from local board policy and the employment contract is correct, and these documents are not in the corpus.
That a nonrenewal notice is a licensure event. Under the corpus, nonrenewal of the employment contract matters for licensure only through PSU reporting duties in LICN-007 §9.

The draft's notes say the grievance timeline comes from local board policy, which the corpus does not contain. The reviewer should not treat the 60-day LICN-007 §3(d) window as applicable to this question.

question: does UCPS pay for CEU courses

answer.reference_answer: The licensure policies in the corpus do not say whether Union County Public Schools pays for CEU courses or any other continuing education cost, so this question cannot be answered from them. What the policies do cover: a CEU is renewal credit equal to two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours of professional development, and a teacher holding a CPL must complete eight CEUs in each five-year renewal cycle, split by grade band. Each PSU must adopt policies ensuring that activities used for renewal credit meet SBE criteria and are appropriate for the educator, and it may add its own continuing education requirements. Any decision on paying for courses would come from UCPS's local policy, which is not in this corpus.

A CEU is renewal credit: one CEU is two-thirds of a semester credit hour from an institution of higher education, or ten clock hours of professional development programming.

For a teacher holding a CPL, the renewal requirement is eight CEUs per five-year renewal cycle, with the split depending on grade band.

question: The teacher took a CEU course from a private provider. Will UCPS accept it as district PD credit for its own salary or evaluation purposes?

answer.reference_answer: The state policies do not say whether Union County Public Schools will accept a private-provider course as district professional development credit for salary or evaluation purposes. That decision belongs to the local school unit. The policies require each school unit to adopt its own procedures so that activities counted toward renewal meet state criteria, and they let the unit consider the direct relationship to the educator's work, any school improvement plan, and state strategic priorities. They also let the unit add its own continuing education requirements. The policies do not address salary credit for professional development (the salary-credit policy covers only experience and degree credit) or how professional development feeds into the evaluation rating. Separately, for the educator's state CPL renewal, the course counts only if it meets the CEU definition (college credit or ten clock hours of professional development programming) and fits the required categories. The policies do not state whether a private provider's course qualifies, so that must be checked against UCPS and DPI guidance that is not in this corpus.

key_points.point: Whether UCPS accepts the course as district PD credit is a local decision. The policies require each school unit to adopt its own procedures for activities counted toward renewal credit, and they let the unit set additional continuing education requirements based on local needs. UCPS's own policy is not in the corpus.

In making that local determination, the unit considers the direct relationship between the activity and the educator's work responsibilities, any school improvement plan in effect for the assigned school, and the State Board's and DPI's strategic priorities.

Salary: the corpus has no rule giving salary credit for continuing education or professional development. The salary-credit policy addresses only experience credit and graduate degree pay, so the policies are silent on this question.

Professional development programs and college credit are the listed sources of CEUs. The corpus does not say whether a private provider's course qualifies, so the answer cannot be confirmed from these policies.

question: My NC CPL lapsed in June and my contract ended. Am I eligible for unemployment benefits through the NC Division of Employment Security?

answer.reference_answer: The LICN policies do not address unemployment benefits or the NC Division of Employment Security's eligibility rules, so the assistant cannot say whether this educator qualifies. The policies do say how an expired CPL is treated: every license expires June 30 of the year it is set to expire unless renewed, and a PSU may ask DPI to validate an expired CPL only if the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year. The policies also say a teacher whose license expires after a non-proficient evaluation without a mandatory improvement plan may apply for an IPL 30 days after receiving notice of expiration. The analyst should direct the benefits question to DES, and should confirm the license facts (expiration date, reason for lapse, and employment history) before relying on any licensure outcome.

key_points.point: The LICN policies do not govern unemployment benefits or DES eligibility, so whether this educator qualifies for unemployment cannot be answered from them.

Under the policies, every license expires June 30 of the calendar year in which it is set to expire unless it is renewed, extended, or converted, so a June lapse is consistent with the general expiration rule, but the policies do not say whether this specific lapse is the result of a missed renewal.

A PSU may request validation of an expired CPL even without the required CEUs, but only if the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year. A validated CPL is effective for three years, and the educator must complete the renewal requirements by the end of the third year to renew for a new five-year cycle.

A teacher whose CPL expires at the end of a renewal cycle after a non-proficient evaluation, without a mandatory improvement plan, may apply for an IPL 30 days after receiving DPI's expiration notice.

Renewal of a teacher CPL requires at least a proficient rating on the most recent annual evaluation for teachers employed by a local board, and completion of eight CEUs in the renewal cycle; the policies do not link these requirements to unemployment status.

A contract ending is reportable to the Superintendent only where the separation involves misconduct or conduct that may justify discipline; the policies do not treat an ordinary contract end as a licensure event, and the PSU must notify the educator of any reporting requirement on separation.

question: Teacher got a Residency License in 2017 under the older rules and is now in year 8 of renewal. Which requirements apply to them: the ones in effect when the RL was issued, or the current ones?

answer.reference_answer: The policies contain no grandfathering or transition rules, and the corpus holds only the currently adopted versions. It cannot confirm what applied in 2017, so it cannot say that rules in force at issuance continue to apply. Current rules govern whatever license the teacher holds now. The premise also doesn't fit the policies: a residency license is a one-year license renewable twice, so it cannot still be in force in year 8, and it can't have a renewal cycle that long. Ask what license the teacher holds now. If it is a CPL, the five-year renewal cycle and the CEU, evaluation and other requirements in LICN-030 and LICN-033 apply. If it is an IPL, it is a three-year nonrenewable license that can convert to a CPL under LICN-024. Check any older-rule or transition question against DPI, since the corpus is silent on it.

key_points.point: A residency license is a one-year license renewable twice, so it lasts at most three years. A 2017 RL cannot still be an RL in year 8, and the 'year 8 of renewal' framing does not match the RL definition.

By June 30 of the third year of the RL, the teacher had to meet the IPL or CPL requirements (including EPP recommendation) for conversion. Otherwise the RL expires, and the IPL or CPL becomes effective only on the date the requirements are satisfied.

The only multi-year 'renewal cycle' defined is the five-year period between renewals of a CPL. Every license expires June 30 of its expiration year unless renewed, extended or converted. If the teacher now holds a CPL, the current renewal requirements apply.

If the teacher holds a CPL, the current renewal rules include eight CEUs, split by grade band. One CEU is two-thirds of a semester credit hour or ten clock hours. A teacher employed by a local board must also show at least a 'proficient' rating on the most recent annual evaluation, as defined in LICN-030 §2(a).

question: Initial Professional License expired in 2019. Applicant wants reinstatement in 2025. Which reinstatement rules apply and does the length of the lapse change anything?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not provide a reinstatement procedure for an expired Initial Professional License, and they set no lapse-length limit that would govern this request. An IPL is a three-year nonrenewable license that expires June 30 unless renewed, extended, or converted, so the 2019 expiration is not something the policies allow to be revived. The only reinstatement procedure (LICN-007 §8) covers licenses revoked or applications denied through discipline, with the 12-month wait running from that action, so it does not apply to a simple expiration. The validation route in LICN-033 §3 covers only expired continuing professional licenses, not IPLs. The practical path is a new IPL application under LICN-020 §1 (NC EPP completion with EPP recommendation, out-of-state EPP, or an out-of-state clear license with fewer than three years of licensed experience), with the LICN-004 disclosures and the LICN-008 fee; the corpus cannot confirm what rules applied in 2019 or whether they changed.

key_points.point: The policy series has no reinstatement procedure for an expired IPL. An IPL is a three-year nonrenewable license, and every license expires June 30 of its expiration year unless it is renewed, extended, or converted under SBE policy.

LICN-020 sets the qualifications for obtaining an IPL and does not provide for reinstating one that has expired. The applicant would need to qualify for a new IPL under one of the three routes listed.

The only reinstatement mechanism in the corpus is LICN-007 §8, which applies to a revoked license or a denied application. The applicant may petition no sooner than 12 months after the effective date of that revocation or denial, in writing to the Superintendent, and the petition may be denied, granted, or granted on probation. An ordinary expiration is not a revocation or denial, so this route does not appear to apply on the facts given.

The validation provision in LICN-033 §3 applies only to an expired continuing professional license, not an IPL. It also requires a PSU governing body request and that the educator was not employed by any PSU during the preceding fiscal year. A validated CPL lasts three years, and validation can occur without the required CEUs.

The policies do not state a maximum lapse length after which an IPL expiration or a new IPL application is barred. The length of the lapse therefore does not change eligibility under these policies. The 12-month waiting period in LICN-007 §8(a) would matter only if the lapse followed a revocation or denial, and it would be measured from that action, not from the 2019 expiration.

A new IPL application requires a complete application under LICN-004, including disclosure of any prior license suspension or revocation and any criminal history not expunged. It also requires the application fee, and the applicant must be cleared of any investigation under LICN-007. For an application to guarantee processing in the fiscal year, it must be submitted by April 15.

The lapse blocks the CPL route as well. A CPL requires holding a current NC IPL or residency license, so the expired IPL cannot be the basis for a CPL. The CEU renewal requirements for teachers apply to holders of a CPL, so the applicant's lack of renewal credits since 2019 is not itself a bar to a new IPL.

missing_facts_to_ask: Did the 2019 IPL simply expire, or was it revoked, suspended, surrendered, or otherwise disciplined? This decides whether LICN-007 §8 could apply.

Did the applicant complete an NC educator preparation program and have it recommend the applicant, or is the EPP out of state?

Was the applicant employed by any PSU in the fiscal year before the request? This matters only if a PSU seeks validation under LICN-033 §3, which applies to CPLs.
Has the applicant passed the applicable licensure examinations?
Does the applicant have any criminal history, pending charges, or prior license discipline that must be disclosed under LICN-004?

question: Master's in school administration finished 2014 at a program that's since been reviewed. Applying for an admin license now. Does the completion date or the program's approval status at the time matter?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not say whether the completion date or the program's approval status at completion or at application controls. answer.reference_answer: The policies set no expiration or validity period for licensure exam scores, so nothing in the corpus says a 2010 pass has aged out. question: Teacher's renewal cycle closed June 30. Some CEUs were completed in July and August after the cycle ended. Which cycle do those count toward?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not say which renewal cycle CEUs completed after June 30 count toward, and the corpus contains no post-June-30 crediting rule or grace period for CEU completion. A CEU is credit for renewal, defined as either two-thirds of a semester credit hour from a higher education institution or ten clock hours of professional development programming. The policies do not tie a CEU's completion date to a particular cycle.

Licenses expire June 30 of the calendar year in which they are set to expire unless renewed, extended, or converted. This is the expiration rule that the question's June 30 date most likely reflects; the policies do not separately define a June 30 cycle close.
Crediting rules for CEUs completed after the cycle ends, including any grace period or allocation to the prior or next cycle, are not addressed anywhere in the corpus.

The only July-dated rule in the corpus is the fee schedule's renewal processing window of 4/15 through 7/31 for renewals processed by the school system. It concerns when renewal may be processed, not which CEUs count toward which cycle, and should not be read as a CEU crediting rule.

If a teacher who meets the Section 1 criteria is not placed on a mandatory improvement plan, the license expires at the end of the renewal cycle, and the teacher may apply for an IPL 30 days after notice of expiration. This matters if the July-August CEUs fail to bring the teacher into compliance.

question: National Board certification earned 2012. Teacher now renewing a CPL in 2025. Does NBC status count the same way under today's renewal rules as it did when it was earned?

answer.reference_answer: The current policy (LICN-033 §2) gives NBC credit by renewal cycle, not by a standing status. Certification gives credit for all eight CEUs in the cycle in which the teacher is certified, and renewing an NBC gives two CEUs in the cycle in which it is renewed. Nothing in the current text says a 2012 certification carries credit into a 2025 renewal cycle, and the policies set no expiration for NBC status. Whether NBC helps the 2025 renewal therefore depends on whether an NBC renewal happened in that cycle, and the policies do not say how NBC was treated when it was earned in 2012. The corpus holds only current rules, and the LICN-030 and LICN-033 versions in it took effect July 1, 2026, after the 2025 renewal, so it cannot confirm what applied in 2012 or 2025.

key_points.point: Under the current rule, NBC certification earns credit for all eight CEUs in the renewal cycle in which the teacher receives certification.
Under the current rule, renewing an NBC earns two CEUs in the renewal cycle in which it is renewed.

The current policies treat NBC credit as tied to a renewal cycle. They set no validity period or expiration for an NBC earned in 2012, and they do not say a 2012 certification carries into the 2025 cycle.

The 2025 renewal still requires the teacher to complete eight CEUs in that cycle, with the grade-band composition in LICN-030. NBC credit may cover this only if an NBC credit or renewal falls within that cycle, and the policies do not say whether NBC credit can satisfy the license-area and literacy components.
The corpus cannot confirm how NBC status counted when earned in 2012 or what rules governed the 2025 renewal. The current LICN-030 and LICN-033 took effect July 1, 2026, after the 2025 renewal.
The teacher also needs a rating of proficient on the most recent annual evaluation to renew a CPL, which NBC status does not address.

question: CTE teacher's industry credential from 2016 may be past its validity window. Teacher is applying for a license in 2025. Does the credential's issue date still count?

answer.reference_answer: The policies do not mention industry credentials, their issue dates, or any validity or age window, so they cannot tell the analyst whether a 2016 industry credential still counts for a 2025 application. What they do cover is the CTE framework: career and technical education is a teacher license area that can be issued to applicants holding only a high school diploma or associate's degree, and CTE license areas and their listed test requirements are set out in the policies. Any credential-specific rule would have to come from the CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual that LICN-003 references, which is not in the corpus, so the analyst should check that manual and confirm with DPI licensure staff. The corpus also cannot confirm which rules applied in 2025, because the current versions take effect in 2025 or 2026.

key_points.point: The policies do not address industry credentials, their issue dates, or any validity window or age limit, so they cannot confirm whether the 2016 credential still counts toward a 2025 application.

Career and Technical Education is a teacher license classification with its own license areas, and an applicant with a high school diploma or associate's degree may be issued a teaching license in CTE areas if the other requirements for the license classification are met.

For CTE license areas, the applicable licensure examination requirements are listed in the policy's testing table (for example Family and Consumer Sciences, Marketing Education, Technology Education, Business Education, and Computer Science and IT Education). The policies do not state that an industry credential substitutes for any listed test, and they refer CTE testing questions to a manual not in the corpus.

Relevant full-time non-teaching industry work experience may be credited toward salary experience on the recommendation of the employing public school unit, subject to documentation and a DPI relevance finding. This is a salary-credit rule and does not make a credential valid or invalid.

For Class V Career-Technical Trade and Industry Education licenses, the policy ties experience credit to completing required training and work experience to qualify for a provisional license. The provisional license rule (LICN-014) is referenced but is not in the corpus.

Date caveat: the corpus holds only current versions, most of which are effective 2026-07-01 (LICN-003 takes effect 2026-09-01; LICN-006 takes effect 2025-07-01). The corpus cannot confirm what rules applied to an application filed in 2025.

missing_facts_to_ask: Which specific CTE license area the teacher is seeking, since the testing table and CTE rules differ by area.
The exact name and issuing body of the 2016 industry credential, and whether it is one of the examinations listed in LICN-003 for the area.
The teacher's highest education level and whether they hold a high school diploma, associate's degree, or bachelor's degree.
Whether the teacher holds any current North Carolina or out-of-state professional educator license, and which classification (IPL, CPL, residency, permit) is being sought.
Whether the teacher is seeking salary experience credit for industry work, and whether the employing PSU has recommended it.
Whether the teacher has taken or passed the required licensure exam for the area.
false_premises: The policies contain an industry credential validity window or issue-date age limit. No such rule appears in the corpus.
An industry credential's issue date is a licensure criterion under these policies. No policy addresses industry credentials at all.
out_of_scope_parts: Whether the 2016 industry credential is still valid under any rule outside this corpus, including the CTE Licensure Policy and Procedures Manual referenced in LICN-003 §5, which is not in the corpus.
Provisional license requirements under LICN-014, which is cited by LICN-010 and LICN-001 but is not in the corpus.
What rules applied to a 2025 application, since the corpus holds only current versions effective in 2025 or 2026.
answer.reviewer_notes: The draft premise assumes a credential validity window that the policies do not contain, so the answer is not_covered for the credential question itself. The CTE framework parts are answerable from LICN-003, LICN-006, and LICN-010, which gives a partial answer. The 2025 filing date predates the current versions' effective dates, so the answer is limited to the current text. LICN-014 and the CTE manual are referenced but absent from the corpus. The question also omits the CTE area, degree, and exam status, which would matter for any follow-up.
